Using an experimental design with five conditions, researchers found that model-based learning outperformed scripted collaboration on process quality and knowledge measures. Results challenge the prevailing positive view of collaboration scripts in CSCL research, suggesting adaptive scripting approaches instead.
evidence_span: title, abstract, methods, findings
coding_notes: Experimental design with five conditions comparing scripted collaboration vs. model-based learning (worked-out examples with elaboration support). Primary focus on dyadic or small-group computer-mediated problem-solving; individual learning outcomes also measured. Sociocultural framing of collaborative learning; socio-cognitive elements in explanation and model observation.

title: The power of natural frameworks: Technology and the question of agency in CSCL settings
authors: Annika Lantz-Andersson
summary_haiku: # Summary This study analyzes how secondary school students frame computer-supported collaborative learning situations using video analysis of mathematics problem-solving with educational software. Results reveal students shift between social frameworks where they assume responsibility for understanding tasks and natural frameworks where they attribute difficulties to technology design. When receiving incorrect feedback without explanation, students often cease engaging with mathematical reasoning and instead attempt procedural workarounds, potentially avoiding accountability for learning while preserving self-esteem.
evidence_span: methods (video analysis of problem-solving) + findings (framework shifts, feedback responses)
coding_notes: Video analysis of moment-by-moment collaborative episodes during mathematics problem-solving is the core methodology. The study examines how students frame situations and respond to technology feedback, grounded in sociocultural and dialogic perspectives on agency and responsibility in collaborative learning.

title: The joint organization of interaction within a multimodal CSCL medium
authors: Alan Zemel & Gerry Stahl
summary_haiku: This ethnomethodological case study examines how three students organize collaborative mathematical problem-solving in a synchronous dual-interaction online environment combining text chat and shared whiteboard. Through sequential interaction analysis, the authors reveal that students co-construct shared mathematical understanding by coordinating visual, narrative, and symbolic representations across media. The indexical field formed by referential links between chat messages and whiteboard drawings establishes common ground, enabling group cognition and deep mathematical learning through multiple realizations of mathematical objects.
evidence_span: title, abstract, methodology description
coding_notes: Ethnomethodological case study with sequential interaction analysis of moment-by-moment collaborative episodes in a multimodal synchronous environment. The focus on indexical fields, referential links, and co-construction of shared understanding across chat and whiteboard aligns with sociocultural and distributed cognition theories. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

title: Affordances revisited: Articulating a Merleau-Pontian view
authors: Nina Bonderup Dohn
summary_haiku: This article develops a Merleau-Pontian account of affordances for CSCL, arguing that existing interpretations within the field contain unresolved ontological and epistemological tensions. The author proposes that affordances are dynamic, relational, and skill-relative properties existing independently of perception but relative to agents' body-schematic interaction potential. This framework shifts design and empirical research focus toward background structuring and learners' developing capabilities rather than mental models.
evidence_span: abstract and conceptual framing
coding_notes: This is a theoretical/philosophical article developing a Merleau-Pontian framework for affordances in CSCL rather than an empirical study. Coded as ethnographic_case_study as the closest fit for qualitative conceptual work, though the article is primarily theoretical. No specific pedagogy, technology, or empirical methodology is described; the focus is on ontological and epistemological foundations for understanding affordances.

title: Genre and CSCL: The form and rhetoric of the online posting
authors: Norm Friesen
summary_haiku: This study applies genre analysis to online discussion postings in CSCL contexts, hypothesizing that educational postings share rhetorical characteristics with their epistolary precursor, the letter. Through content analysis of 136 postings, the author identifies 240 rhetorical markers reflecting epistolary dynamics, including salutations, present-tense references, and temporal references. Findings suggest that cultural and historical factors embedded in familiar genres significantly shape how students engage in online collaborative learning, beyond technological affordances alone.
evidence_span: methods (content analysis of 136 postings, 240 rhetorical markers) + findings (epistolary characteristics identified)
coding_notes: Study employs systematic coding of rhetorical markers in online postings (content analysis) combined with linguistic/genre-based interpretation (discourse analysis). Primary unit is the posting artifact itself. Dialogic theory frames meaning-making through genre conventions; sociocultural perspective emphasizes cultural/historical shaping of participation. No explicit pedagogy model is foregrounded; focus is on form and rhetoric rather than instructional design.

title: Exploring metaskills of knowledge-creating inquiry in higher education
authors: Hanni Muukkonen & Minna Lakkala
summary_haiku: This study investigates metaskills required for knowledge-creating inquiry in higher education through an 11-week undergraduate psychology course using progressive inquiry and web-based collaboration. Qualitative analysis of database discourse and student self-reflections revealed three student groups exhibited varying engagement levels in collaborative object-oriented inquiry. Group C demonstrated superior skills in monitoring individual, collective, and object-oriented aspects of inquiry, while Groups A and B struggled with shared knowledge advancement. Findings suggest metaskills for collaborative knowledge creation develop through sustained socialization into inquiry practices emphasizing iterative development of shared epistemic objects.
evidence_span: methods (qualitative analysis of database discourse and self-reflections) + findings (three student groups, metaskills development)
coding_notes: Study employs systematic coding of discourse and reflections across student groups in a progressive inquiry setting, aligned with knowledge-building pedagogy. Web-based collaboration platform (likely Knowledge Forum or similar wiki-based tool) supports asynchronous knowledge construction. Confidence slightly reduced due to limited methodological detail in excerpt, but core approach is clearly qualitative content/discourse analysis of collaborative artifacts.

title: A knowledge-practice perspective on technology-mediated learning
authors: Kai Hakkarainen
summary_haiku: Technology enhances learning through transformed social practices, not merely through tool implementation. While knowledge-building theory emphasizes idea advancement, this perspective argues that genuine educational transformation requires cultivating epistemic practices—socially embedded ways of working with knowledge—that channel intellectual efforts toward collective knowledge advancement. Material artifacts and social practices constitute dialectical unity in knowledge creation.
evidence_span: title, abstract, theoretical framing
coding_notes: Hakkarainen's 2009 work is a theoretical perspective piece emphasizing epistemic practices and knowledge-building communities. Methodology is inferred as ethnographic/case-study oriented given focus on socially embedded practices; technology is inferred as knowledge-base/wiki-like given knowledge-building emphasis, though the article may be primarily conceptual rather than empirical.

title: Time is precious: Variable- and event-centred approaches to process analysis in CSCL research
authors: Peter Reimann
summary_haiku: CSCL research often neglects temporal dimensions despite studying processes unfolding over weeks or months. Reimann argues that variable-centered variance theory inadequately captures long-term change, proposing event-centered analysis as a complementary approach. Event-based methods enable narrative explanation, accommodate multiple causality types, and facilitate integration of qualitative and quantitative analyses, offering CSCL researchers more appropriate tools for analyzing extended collaborative learning processes.
evidence_span: abstract, title, and conceptual framing
coding_notes: Reimann's paper is a methodological treatise proposing event-centered temporal analysis as an alternative to variable-centered approaches for CSCL. The focus on sequential, narrative explanation of unfolding processes aligns with sequence/process mining and discourse analysis. Activity theory's emphasis on contradictions and temporal development of activity systems fits the temporal-developmental lens. Confidence is moderate because the paper is primarily theoretical/methodological rather than an empirical study; no specific technology or pedagogy is the focus.

title: Distinguishing knowledge-sharing, knowledge- construction, and knowledge-creation discourses
authors: Jan van Aalst
summary_haiku: This study distinguishes three discourse modes—knowledge sharing, knowledge construction, and knowledge creation—using a coding scheme applied to secondary students' asynchronous online discussions in Knowledge Forum about SARS and Avian Flu. Analysis of four student groups' discourses revealed one group engaged in knowledge-creation discourse with superior knowledge advancement, one in knowledge-sharing discourse, and two in hybrid modes. Community sense emerged as the primary differentiating factor.
evidence_span: methods (coding scheme applied to asynchronous discussions) + findings (discourse mode analysis across four groups)
coding_notes: Study applies systematic coding scheme to distinguish three discourse modes in Knowledge Forum posts, making content_analysis primary with discourse_analysis as secondary. Knowledge-building theory and Knowledge Forum platform are central. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

title: A three-level analysis of collaborative learning in dual-interaction spaces
authors: Jacques Lonchamp
summary_haiku: This article presents a three-level qualitative interaction analysis methodology for dual-interaction spaces—CSCL systems combining shared artifact editing with synchronous communication. The approach analyzes collaborative learning traces at dialog, knowledge, and action levels to identify patterns and inform system customization. Applied to software engineering diagram construction, the method reveals how learners negotiate categorization rules through prototypical examples, enabling evidence-based improvements to learning environment design.
evidence_span: title, abstract, methodology description
coding_notes: The three-level qualitative interaction analysis (dialog, knowledge, action) is the defining methodological contribution. The dual-interaction space (shared artifact + synchronous communication) and focus on negotiation of categorization rules through examples align with sociocultural and dialogic frameworks. No AI/LLM involvement evident.

title: Collaborative corrections with spelling control: Digital resources and peer assistance
authors: Asta Cekaite
summary_haiku: Swedish eighth-graders collaboratively corrected spelling errors using Microsoft Word's spellchecker during English writing tasks. Through conversation analysis of video-recorded sessions, the study identified how diagnostic tools and spelling lists configured different correction practices. Students preferentially used diagnostic feedback for autonomous problem-solving before requesting peer assistance or spelling suggestions, demonstrating that underspecified software instructions created space for creative collaborative engagement and language learning.
evidence_span: methods (conversation analysis, video-recorded sessions) + findings (correction practices, peer assistance patterns)
coding_notes: Cekaite's study uses fine-grained conversation analysis of video-recorded collaborative episodes to examine how students interact with spelling feedback and each other. The primary focus is peer-assisted correction during shared writing, with Microsoft Word's spellchecker as a diagnostic tool that scaffolds but does not determine interaction.

title: Web 2.0: Inherent tensions and evident challenges for education
authors: Nina Bonderup Dohn
summary_haiku: Web 2.0 practices and educational systems embody fundamentally incompatible learning metaphors. While Web 2.0 emphasizes participatory, distributed knowledge construction with internal goals, education prioritizes individual knowledge acquisition for external purposes. This conceptual tension manifests practically in challenges regarding collaboration, evaluation criteria, and material authenticity when Web 2.0 tools are integrated into educational settings.
evidence_span: abstract and conceptual framing
coding_notes: This is a conceptual/theoretical paper examining tensions between Web 2.0 epistemologies and educational systems rather than an empirical study. Primary methodology coded as ethnographic_case_study as a best-fit for qualitative critical analysis of situated practices; secondary content_analysis reflects systematic examination of how Web 2.0 and education embody different learning metaphors. Confidence moderate due to lack of explicit methods section indicating actual data collection or analysis procedures.

title: Wikis to support the “collaborative” part of collaborative learning
authors: Johann Ari Larusson & Richard Alterman
summary_haiku: Wikis provide an effective platform for supporting asynchronous, non-collocated collaborative learning when enhanced with awareness, navigation, and communication components. Two case studies demonstrate that prefabricated wiki structures function as coordinating representations, enabling both tightly coupled team design projects and loosely coupled co-blogging activities to maintain adequate intersubjective spaces for productive student collaboration.
evidence_span: title, abstract, case study design description
coding_notes: The study uses two bounded case studies of wiki-supported collaborative learning; methodology is qualitative but not explicitly ethnographic. Prefabricated wiki structures function as collaboration scripts; awareness and navigation components support orchestration. No AI/LLM involvement evident.

title: Earth science learning in SMALLab: A design experiment for mixed reality
authors: David Birchfield & Colleen Megowan-Romanowicz
summary_haiku: This design experiment examined how mixed-reality environments support collaborative earth science learning. Researchers implemented SMALLab, a semi-immersive platform enabling colocated students to interact face-to-face within computationally mediated spaces. A 3-day intervention with 72 high school students revealed significantly increased student-to-student exchanges compared to traditional instruction and notable achievement gains on concept assessments, suggesting mixed-reality technology's potential for enhancing K-12 collaborative learning when properly designed.
evidence_span: title, abstract, methods, findings
coding_notes: Design experiment with iterative intervention (SMALLab) in naturalistic classroom setting; mixed-reality platform is a tangible/spatial interface supporting colocated face-to-face collaboration. Achievement gains and interaction patterns suggest learning analytics component, though primary framing is design-based research testing the intervention's efficacy.

title: Contrasting the use of tools for presentation and critique: Some cases from architectural education
authors: Gustav Lymer & Jonas Ivarsson & Oskar Lindwall
summary_haiku: This ethnomethodological video analysis of architectural design reviews examines how presentation technologies shape critique practices. Comparing poster-based, digital slideshow, and hybrid setups across 143 sessions, the study reveals that digital technologies fundamentally transform sequential organization, shared attention, and part-whole relations during discussion and assessment. The findings suggest that presentation tools designed primarily for delivery may inadequately support subsequent critique, highlighting the need for spatially organized interfaces better suited to collaborative design review practices.
evidence_span: methods (ethnomethodological video analysis, 143 sessions), findings (sequential organization, shared attention, part-whole relations)
coding_notes: Study employs fine-grained video analysis of design review interactions, examining how presentation tools (posters, slides, hybrid) shape collaborative critique practices. Primary focus is on moment-by-moment discourse and artifact use rather than learning outcomes, fitting interaction_analysis; secondary methods include ethnographic observation and systematic coding of presentation modalities.

title: An ontology engineering approach to the realization of theory-driven group formation
authors: Seiji Isotani & Akiko Inaba & Mitsuru Ikeda & Riichiro Mizoguchi
summary_haiku: This research presents an ontology-based framework for theory-driven group formation in collaborative learning. Using ontological engineering, the authors formalize learning theory concepts to guide group composition, role assignment, and activity design. A proof-of-concept experiment with four instructors and twenty participants demonstrated that groups formed according to pedagogical theory specifications showed significantly better performance and more meaningful interactions than control groups, suggesting ontologies effectively operationalize learning theories for improved collaborative learning outcomes.
evidence_span: title, abstract, methods, findings
coding_notes: The study uses ontological engineering to formalize and operationalize learning theory for group formation and role assignment—a form of structured collaboration scripting. The proof-of-concept experiment with control comparison and performance/interaction metrics indicates experimental design. Sociocultural theory underpins the theory-driven approach to collaborative learning; activity theory is secondary given the focus on formalizing activity structures via ontology.

title: A framework for conceptualizing, representing, and analyzing distributed interaction
authors: Daniel D. Suthers & Nathan Dwyer & Richard Medina & Ravi Vatrapu
summary_haiku: # Summary Suthers and colleagues present an uptake analysis framework for analyzing distributed technology-mediated interaction. The framework uses contingency graphs—abstract transcripts representing events as vertices and relationships between events as edges—to unify interaction data across multiple media and temporal scales. Uptake, defined as participants taking prior events as relevant for ongoing activity, serves as the conceptual foundation. The authors demonstrate the framework's utility through qualitative and quantitative analyses of synchronous and asynchronous collaborative learning data, arguing it enables both microanalysis and scaled statistical analysis while supporting dialogue across diverse CSCL methodologies.
evidence_span: abstract, methods, framework description
coding_notes: This is a methodological framework paper rather than a pedagogical intervention study. Uptake analysis is fundamentally a discourse-analytic approach using contingency graphs to represent interaction events and their relationships. The framework is technology-agnostic but demonstrated on synchronous and asynchronous CSCL data; primary technology coded as shared_workspace_canvas as a representative example, though the framework applies across media.

title: Computer-supported argumentation: A review of the state of the art
authors: Oliver Scheuer & Frank Loll & Niels Pinkwart & Bruce M. McLaren
summary_haiku: Computer-supported argumentation systems have evolved over 15-20 years to support and teach argumentation skills across domains. This literature review examines 50 systems, analyzing argument representations, interaction designs, ontologies, automated analysis techniques, and empirical findings. Key results show that visual representations and structured interaction designs improve argumentative discourse, while macro-level pedagogical scripts enhance learning outcomes. However, conflicting empirical results reveal the need for comprehensive theoretical frameworks and systematic comparative studies.
evidence_span: title, abstract, review scope (50 systems analyzed)
coding_notes: This is a systematic literature review of computer-supported argumentation systems. The primary methodology is content analysis of 50 existing systems and their empirical studies. Unit of analysis is the artifact/discourse traces (argument representations, interaction designs) and classroom outcomes. Pedagogy centers on argumentation with structured scripts. Technology spans visual representations and structured interaction designs. Theory is dialogic (multi-voiced argument construction) and sociocultural. No AI/LLM involvement in the systems reviewed (2010 publication predates modern LLMs).

title: Exploring whether students’ use of labelling depends upon the type of activity
authors: Eva Mary Bures & Philip C. Abrami & Richard F. Schmid
summary_haiku: This mixed-methods study examined whether graduate students use labeling features less frequently during structured versus unstructured online dialogue. Participants (n=37) engaged in two activities: an unstructured discussion and a HipBone Game with predetermined structure. Results showed significantly reduced label usage during the structured activity, with 62% using labels multiple times unstructured versus 46% structured. Students preferred the structured dialogue but reported mixed satisfaction with labeling. Findings suggest structured activities provide alternative scaffolding, potentially rendering labeling features redundant.
evidence_span: methods (mixed-methods design, n=37, two activities) + findings (62% vs 46% label usage, preference data, satisfaction reports)
coding_notes: Study compares structured (HipBone Game) versus unstructured dialogue, measuring labeling behavior quantitatively (frequencies, significance testing) and qualitatively (satisfaction, preference). Mixed methods combines both; collaboration scripts and teacher orchestration reflect the pedagogical scaffolding contrast. Sociocultural framing emphasizes how structure mediates tool use in dialogue.

title: Toward a dialectic relation between the results in CSCL: Three critical methodological aspects of content analysis schemes
authors: Marc Clara & Teresa Mauri
summary_haiku: This paper proposes a framework of indicators based on three critical methodological aspects—units of analysis, relations between theoretical levels, and dimensions of analysis—to facilitate reciprocal positioning of content analysis results in CSCL research. Rather than seeking theoretical integration across diverse approaches, the authors argue for dialectical relations that reveal tensions and enable mutual theoretical development within the field's inherent methodological diversity.
evidence_span: title, abstract, summary
coding_notes: This is a methodological paper proposing a framework for content analysis schemes in CSCL rather than reporting an empirical study. Primary focus is on systematizing how to code and relate units of analysis across theoretical levels; no specific pedagogy or technology is instantiated. Sociocultural and dialogic theories underpin the emphasis on discourse and collaborative meaning-making.

title: Mr. Vetro: A Collective Simulation for teaching health science
authors: Andri Ioannidou & Alexander Repenning & David Webb & Diane Keyser & Lisa Luhn & Christof Daetwyler
summary_haiku: Mr. Vetro is a collective simulation where students collaboratively control physiological organs on networked computers to learn about system interactions. Formal evaluation across 400 high school students demonstrated significant learning gains in physiological knowledge and vocabulary, increased inquiry-based teaching practices, and positive real-life health behavior changes, though attitudes toward science remained relatively stable.
evidence_span: methods+findings
coding_notes: Mr. Vetro is a networked collaborative simulation where students collectively control physiological systems, suggesting shared workspace technology and inquiry-based pedagogy. The formal evaluation across 400 students with learning gains indicates experimental/quasi-experimental design with classroom cohorts as primary unit; individual learning outcomes also measured. No AI/LLM involvement evident in 2010 context.

title: Animation and grammar in science education: Learners’ construal of animated educational software
authors: Goran Karlsson
summary_haiku: This case study examines how two upper-secondary students collaboratively interpret animated biochemical processes through written reports. Using interaction analysis of video-recorded sessions, the research reveals that students' grammatically constructed narratives prioritize perceptually salient animated features as active subjects, deriving noun phrases from animation and educational text while substituting verbs with everyday language. Without sufficient subject-matter knowledge, students cannot evaluate adequacy and rely solely on grammatical correctness, resulting in non-scientific explanations. The findings emphasize that technology-supported science education requires consideration of both cultural and semiotic processes.
evidence_span: methods (interaction analysis of video-recorded sessions) + findings (grammatical construction patterns, noun/verb substitution)
coding_notes: The study employs micro-analytic interaction analysis of collaborative interpretation episodes, with secondary content analysis of written reports and grammatical structures. While animation software is present, the focus is on how students interpret it through language rather than on the technology itself; the primary analytical lens is semiotic and linguistic construction of meaning in dialogue.

title: Scripting a distance-learning university course: Do students benefit from net-based scripted collaboration?
authors: Joerg M. Haake & Hans-Rudiger Pfister
summary_haiku: This experimental field study examined whether scripted collaboration benefits net-based learning in a semester-long university operating systems course. Forty-two student groups performed brainstorming, clustering, and essay-writing tasks either with system-enforced scripts or non-scripted instructions. Results showed no general advantage of scripting for knowledge acquisition or task performance. However, principal component analysis revealed scripting slightly improved essay coherence and comprehensibility, suggesting benefits for complex tasks requiring deeper understanding.
evidence_span: title, abstract, methods, results
coding_notes: Clear experimental design comparing scripted vs. non-scripted conditions across 42 groups in a distance-learning setting. Principal component analysis used to assess essay quality; scripting is the core pedagogical intervention. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

title: Distributed leadership in online groups
authors: Julia Gressick & Sharon J. Derry
summary_haiku: In an asynchronous online learning environment, pre-service teachers working in small groups demonstrated highly distributed leadership across all members, with different leadership forms showing varying distribution patterns. While successful group performance was not directly predicted by overall leadership distribution patterns, qualitative analysis revealed that effective groups developed internal organizational structures and positive interpersonal dynamics that facilitated both peer and instructor engagement, suggesting emergent distributed leadership offers a viable alternative to scripted collaborative roles.
evidence_span: title, abstract, and summary indicating qualitative analysis of group interaction patterns and leadership distribution
coding_notes: The study examines how leadership emerges and distributes across small group members in asynchronous online settings through qualitative analysis of group dynamics and discourse. Distributed cognition is the primary theoretical lens because leadership and decision-making are treated as emergent properties distributed across group members rather than localized in individuals. Self-peer regulation is primary pedagogy because groups self-organize their internal structures and roles without scripted assignment, though collaboration scripts are secondary as a point of contrast.

title: Promoting metacognitive skills through peer scaffolding in a CSCL environment
authors: Manoli Pifarre & Ruth Cobos
summary_haiku: A longitudinal case study of 18 university students using the KnowCat knowledge-building system over two semesters examined how peer scaffolding develops metacognitive skills in computer-supported collaborative learning. Content analysis of student annotations revealed statistically significant increases in metacognitive processes, particularly in monitoring and clarity-seeking behaviors. Results suggest pedagogical use of CSCL environments with structured peer feedback effectively enhances students' self-regulation and collaborative problem-solving capabilities.
evidence_span: methods (content analysis of annotations), findings (statistically significant increases in metacognitive processes)
coding_notes: Study employs systematic coding of student annotations (content analysis) with descriptive statistics on metacognitive indicators. KnowCat is a knowledge-building system supporting collaborative annotation and peer feedback. Peer scaffolding and self-regulation align with sociocultural and socio-cognitive frameworks; longitudinal case study design supports the primary methodology choice.

title: Online moderation of synchronous e-argumentation
authors: Christa S. C. Asterhan
summary_haiku: This exploratory study examines effective online moderation of synchronous small-group argumentation in co-located classrooms. Through student questionnaires and protocol analyses of moderated discussions using Digalo software, researchers found that generic scaffolding prompts—effective in face-to-face settings—were ineffective in synchronous e-discussions. Instead, content-specific, involved moderation styles that disguised scaffolding as peer participation proved more effective and appreciated by students.
evidence_span: methods (protocol analysis, questionnaires) + findings (moderation styles, scaffolding effectiveness)
coding_notes: Study uses protocol analysis of synchronous e-discussions (Digalo software) to examine moment-by-moment moderation moves during small-group argumentation. Content-specific scaffolding coded as effective pedagogical strategy; sociocultural framing evident in emphasis on peer participation and social mediation of learning.

title: Scaffolding problem-based learning with CSCL tools
authors: Jingyan Lu & Susanne P. Lajoie & Jeffrey Wiseman
summary_haiku: Interactive whiteboards fundamentally altered teacher scaffolding in medical problem-based learning. This case study compared traditional whiteboard versus interactive whiteboard conditions during deteriorating patient simulations with medical students. Results revealed that interactive whiteboards enabled teachers to visualize all student groups' work simultaneously, allowing them to increase problem complexity and reduce task-structuring guidance. Technology expanded scaffolding choices by externalizing collaborative problem-solving processes.
evidence_span: methods (case study design, conditions), findings (scaffolding differences, teacher awareness)
coding_notes: Study compares two conditions (traditional vs. interactive whiteboard) in a medical PBL context, making it quasi-experimental. Interactive whiteboard functions as both shared workspace and awareness tool, enabling teachers to visualize and adapt scaffolding dynamically. Sociocultural framing emphasizes teacher mediation and externalization of collaborative processes.

title: How digital concept maps about the collaborators’ knowledge and information influence computer-supported collaborative problem solving
authors: Tanja Engelmann & Friedrich W. Hesse
summary_haiku: Digital concept maps displaying collaborators' knowledge structures and information resources enhance computer-supported collaborative problem-solving. This experimental study compared 40 triads—20 with access to partners' concept maps and 20 without—on problem-solving tasks. Results demonstrated that groups with map access acquired greater knowledge-and-information awareness, focused on problem-relevant information, and solved problems faster and more accurately than control groups.
evidence_span: methods (experimental design, 40 triads, control/treatment groups) + findings (knowledge-information awareness, problem-solving speed and accuracy)
coding_notes: Controlled comparison of triads with and without concept map awareness tools; concept maps function as awareness dashboards making collaborators' knowledge structures visible, supporting distributed cognition and self-regulation of collaborative problem-solving.

title: S-COL: A Copernican turn for the development of flexibly reusable collaboration scripts
authors: Christof Wecker & Karsten Stegmann & Florian Bernstein & Michael J. Huber & Georg Kalus & Ingo Kollar & Sabine Rathmayer & Frank Fischer
summary_haiku: S-COL is a browser-based tool enabling flexible reuse of collaboration scripts across diverse web-based learning platforms. Rather than embedding scripts within specific platforms, S-COL implements scripts in the browser and triggers them by recognizing functionally equivalent page types. An empirical study demonstrated that a collaboration script for online search implemented in S-COL effectively increased students' engagement in early-stage search activities, supporting the tool's feasibility for sustainable script development and reuse.
evidence_span: methods + findings
coding_notes: S-COL is a browser-based tool implementing collaboration scripts flexibly across platforms. The empirical study compares script-supported vs. control conditions, measuring engagement in search activities. Primary focus is on script design and reusability; secondary unit includes dyadic/small-group interaction during collaborative search.

title: Revealing preconditions for trustful collaboration in CSCL
authors: Anne Gerdes
summary_haiku: This philosophical analysis examines preconditions for trust in virtual learning environments. Through phenomenological inquiry and case analysis, the author argues that self-surrender—fundamental to human communication—is undermined by surveillance and impression management in online learning systems. Drawing on open-source community models, the study concludes that volunteerism, self-articulation of goals, and inquiry-based teaching methods can foster mastery-oriented learning and authentic collaborative engagement.
evidence_span: abstract, theoretical framing, case analysis
coding_notes: This is primarily a philosophical and phenomenological analysis rather than empirical CSCL research. The case analysis of open-source communities and virtual learning environments suggests ethnographic orientation, but the work is conceptual. Sociocultural and dialogic theories underpin the trust-and-communication argument; critical pragmatic lens evident in concerns about surveillance and power dynamics.

title: Can the interactive whiteboard support young children’s collaborative communication and thinking in classroom science activities?
authors: Ruth Kershner & Neil Mercer & Paul Warwick & Judith Kleine Staarman
summary_haiku: Interactive whiteboards can support young children's collaborative communication and thinking in primary science, but effectiveness depends on multiple interacting factors. Through observational analysis of twelve classrooms, researchers found the IWB facilitates productive dialogue when combined with teacher scaffolding, established "talk rules," and appropriate classroom participation structures. However, the technology alone is not pedagogically transformative; success requires careful integration with other classroom resources and attention to both social and cognitive dimensions of collaborative learning.
evidence_span: methods (observational analysis of 12 classrooms) + findings (IWB effectiveness depends on scaffolding, talk rules, participation structures)
coding_notes: Study emphasizes micro-analytic observation of classroom dialogue and teacher orchestration around IWB use. Primary focus on how technology mediates collaborative communication within established social structures; dialogic and sociocultural theories align with emphasis on talk rules and scaffolded dialogue.

title: Sharing and cultivating tacit knowledge in an online learning environment
authors: Meng Yew Tee
summary_haiku: Online graduate business students cultivated tacit knowledge through a strategic management course using naturalistic inquiry methodology. The course combined readings, threaded discussions, and a simulation game, creating a "ba" (shared context) that encouraged socialization, externalization, combination, and internalization processes aligned with Nonaka's knowledge creation model. Students reported learning tacit dimensions impossible to acquire from textbooks alone.
evidence_span: methods (naturalistic inquiry, course design) + findings (tacit knowledge cultivation, SECI processes)
coding_notes: Naturalistic inquiry with in-depth study of a bounded online course context suggests ethnographic case study; explicit use of Nonaka's knowledge creation model (SECI) and 'ba' concept anchors knowledge_building_theory as primary. Threaded discussions and simulation game indicate asynchronous forum + shared workspace; cohort-level analysis of tacit knowledge cultivation is primary unit, though individual learning outcomes are also examined.

title: Using activity theory to understand intergenerational play: The case of Family Quest
authors: Sinem Siyahhan & Sasha A. Barab & Michael P. Downton
summary_haiku: # Summary This study examined intergenerational play between parents and children (ages 9-13) using Quest Atlantis, an educational 3D game, through activity theory analysis. Five-week observations of seven parent-child dyads revealed that successful collaborative gaming required shared intentions and expertise exchange. While outcomes varied across dyads, the research demonstrated that educational video games can facilitate meaningful family bonding and learning, particularly when designed to encourage parents and children to leverage complementary skills around personally relevant narratives.
evidence_span: title, summary, methods (five-week observations of dyads), findings (shared intentions, expertise exchange)
coding_notes: Activity theory is explicitly named in the title and framing. The five-week observational study of seven parent-child dyads in a bounded 3D game environment is characteristic of ethnographic case study with micro-level interaction analysis. Quest Atlantis is a shared digital workspace where dyads collaborate on quests.

title: The collaborative construction of chronotopes during computer-supported collaborative professional tasks
authors: Maria Beatrice Ligorio & Giuseppe Ritella
summary_haiku: # Summary This study analyzes how teachers collaboratively construct spatial and temporal frameworks during computer-supported professional planning using qualitative video analysis of six sessions. The researchers identified three distinct chronotopes—Adagio, Andante, and Allegretto—representing different interaction tempos shaped by tool features, activity complexity, and participant expertise. Results demonstrate that technology mediates collaboration by creating multiple overlapping spaces where different types of coordination emerge, revealing how space-time co-construction fundamentally influences group professional work.
evidence_span: methods (video analysis of six sessions) + findings (chronotope identification and interaction tempo patterns)
coding_notes: Study employs fine-grained qualitative video analysis of collaborative professional planning sessions, identifying emergent temporal-spatial structures (chronotopes). Primary methodology is interaction_analysis due to micro-analytic focus on moment-by-moment coordination; secondary methods include discourse_analysis (linguistic/rhetorical patterns) and ethnographic_case_study (bounded, naturalistic observation). Sociocultural theory frames learning as mediated by tool features and social interaction; activity_theory and distributed_cognition are secondary lenses for understanding how space-time and artifacts shape coordination.

title: The Singapore experience: Synergy of national policy, classroom practice and design research
authors: Chee-Kit Looi & Hyo-Jeong So & Yancy Toh & Wenli Chen
summary_haiku: Singapore's systemic approach to CSCL integration demonstrates how design research methodology bridges macro-level policy, meso-level school implementation, and micro-level classroom interactions. Through the GroupScribbles project across multiple schools, researchers co-designed collaborative learning activities with teachers, developed design principles for rapid collaborative knowledge improvement, and achieved sustainable adoption. This multi-level alignment of policy, practice, and research provides a model for scaling CSCL innovations while addressing real classroom constraints.
evidence_span: title, abstract, summary describing design research across policy-practice-classroom levels
coding_notes: Design-based research is the primary methodology, iteratively refining CSCL interventions (GroupScribbles) across multiple schools. The study explicitly bridges macro (policy), meso (school), and micro (classroom) levels, making cross-level multilevel analysis central. Knowledge building theory and sociocultural framing align with the focus on collaborative knowledge improvement and co-design with teachers.

title: Temporality matters: Advancing a method for analyzing problem-solving processes in a computer-supported collaborative environment
authors: Manu Kapur
summary_haiku: This study advances Lag-sequential Analysis (LsA) as a quantitative method for examining temporal patterns in computer-supported collaborative learning groups. Applied to synchronous online problem-solving discussions, LsA revealed significant sequential interaction patterns invisible to traditional "coding and counting" approaches. Critically, temporal transition patterns between process categories emerged as the strongest predictor of group performance, demonstrating that analyzing the order and sequence of collaborative interactions—not merely their frequency—is essential for understanding collaborative learning processes.
evidence_span: title, abstract, methods, findings
coding_notes: Lag-sequential Analysis is a temporal pattern-extraction method that examines sequential transitions in coded interaction data. The study emphasizes temporal ordering and sequence over frequency counts, making sequence_process_mining the primary methodology. Interaction_analysis is secondary because the underlying data are coded collaborative episodes. Sociocultural theory is primary given the focus on collaborative problem-solving processes in a mediated environment.

title: Learning the physics of electricity: A qualitative analysis of collaborative processes involved in productive failure
authors: Suneeta A. Pathak & Beaumie Kim & Michael J. Jacobson & Baohui Zhang
summary_haiku: This qualitative study examines collaborative problem-solving dynamics in physics education using computer-supported learning. Two student dyads—one experiencing productive failure through initial low-structured activities followed by high-structured ones, and another receiving only high-structured activities—solved electricity problems using NetLogo models. Analysis of video, screen captures, and solutions revealed that initial struggle enabled deeper engagement with the model and reflective reasoning, while over-scripted activities hindered meaningful collaboration and conceptual understanding.
evidence_span: methods (video, screen captures, qualitative analysis) + findings (collaborative dynamics, productive failure effects)
coding_notes: Study employs micro-analytic coding of moment-by-moment collaborative episodes (interaction_analysis) supplemented by case-study depth and systematic coding of artifacts. NetLogo is a shared computational workspace; the core comparison contrasts low-structure (productive failure) versus high-structure (scripted) conditions, grounded in sociocultural and socio-cognitive theories of learning through struggle and explanation.

title: Exploring e-learners’ perceptions of net-based peer-reviewed English writing
authors: Zi-gang Ge
summary_haiku: This study examined asynchronous, blind peer review for improving Chinese adult e-learners' English writing. Thirty-six students divided into three ability groups participated in a year-long experiment with rotating cross-group peer reviews mediated by the instructor. Results showed all groups improved, with lower-ability students making greater progress than higher-ability students. However, high-ability students became discouraged when paired with lower-ability peers for extended periods, suggesting flexible grouping strategies may be necessary.
evidence_span: methods (year-long experiment, three ability groups, rotating cross-group peer reviews) + findings (improvement patterns by ability level, discouragement effects)
coding_notes: Study uses a quasi-experimental design with ability-based grouping and rotating peer-review conditions over time. Primary focus is individual writing improvement and group dynamics; asynchronous peer review is the core technology. Sociocultural framing (peer interaction mediating learning) with socio-cognitive elements (ability-based pairing effects).

title: The logic of wikis: The possibilities of the Web 2.0 classroom
authors: Michael Glassman & Min Ju Kang
summary_haiku: Web 2.0 tools like wikis and blogs can enable Dewey's vision of democratic education by supporting abductive reasoning—the logic of hypothesis generation essential for creative problem-solving. Unlike traditional deductive approaches emphasizing certainty, abduction requires simultaneously maintaining multiple competing premises, a capability previously impossible in classrooms but now feasible through hypertext-based technologies that create scale-free networks of interconnected information nodes.
evidence_span: abstract and conceptual framing
coding_notes: This is a theoretical/conceptual paper articulating how Web 2.0 wikis enable abductive reasoning and Deweyan democratic education. No empirical methodology (experiment, ethnography, or systematic analysis) is evident from the summary; the primary contribution is philosophical/theoretical. Coded as artifact_discourse_trace because wikis themselves are the focal object, with classroom_cohort as secondary context. Sociocultural and distributed cognition theories align with the emphasis on collaborative knowledge networks.

title: Perspective taking and synchronous argumentation for learning the day/night cycle
authors: Baruch B. Schwarz & Yaron Schur & Haim Pensso & Naama Tayer
summary_haiku: Combining perspective-taking through pictures and synchronous computer-supported argumentation promotes conceptual learning of the day/night cycle in Grade 8 students. Using the Digalo tool and design-research methodology with pre-post testing, the study found significant improvements in mental models, elaboration, and knowledge integration. However, teacher mediation during small-group discussions did not enhance learning outcomes, suggesting that meticulous task design and peer argumentation were primary drivers of conceptual change.
evidence_span: methods (design-research, pre-post testing, Digalo tool, small-group discussions) + findings (significant improvements in mental models, elaboration, knowledge integration; teacher mediation effect)
coding_notes: Study employs design-based research with experimental comparison (pre-post testing) of a synchronous argumentation intervention using Digalo. Primary focus is peer argumentation and perspective-taking in small groups; socio-cognitive theory aligns with collaborative conflict driving conceptual change, while dialogic theory captures the multi-voiced argumentation process.

title: Bridging research and practice: Implementing and sustaining knowledge building in Hong Kong classrooms
authors: Carol K. K. Chan
summary_haiku: # Summary This article examines how computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) research translates into classroom practice through a case study of knowledge-building implementation in Hong Kong schools. Using design-based research across macro (policy), meso (teacher networks), and micro (classroom) levels, the study identifies three critical themes: systemic alignment across educational levels, capacity building through principle-based teacher communities, and innovation as continuous inquiry. Findings demonstrate that sustained CSCL adoption requires coordinating institutional policies, teacher professional development networks, and classroom design while adapting research models to local socio-cultural contexts.
evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (design-based research across macro/meso/micro levels), findings (systemic alignment, teacher networks, classroom design)
coding_notes: The article explicitly frames knowledge building (Scardamalia & Bereiter) as the pedagogical model and uses design-based research iteratively across institutional, teacher-community, and classroom levels. Cross-level analysis is central to understanding how CSCL research translates into sustained practice. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

title: Wiki-supported collaborative learning in primary education: How a dialogic space is created for thinking together
authors: Manoli Pifarre & Judith Kleine Staarman
summary_haiku: This study examined how wikis support primary students' collaborative knowledge construction through a dialogic lens. Twenty-five students engaged in a science project using MediaWiki, combining asynchronous wiki interaction with synchronous face-to-face collaboration. Analysis revealed students developed exploratory, cumulative, and disputational talk patterns, establishing intersubjective understanding. The collaborative wiki text demonstrated greater complexity, length, and reasoning than initial individual proposals, supporting the claim that dialogic approaches enhance wiki-based collaborative learning.
evidence_span: methods, findings, discussion of talk patterns and wiki text analysis
coding_notes: Study uses micro-analytic coding of collaborative episodes (exploratory, cumulative, disputational talk) combined with systematic analysis of wiki artifacts. Dialogic lens and focus on intersubjective understanding through multi-voiced dialogue align with dialogic theory; sociocultural framing evident in mediation through wiki technology and face-to-face interaction.

title: An information processing perspective on divergence and convergence in collaborative learning
authors: Robert L. Jorczak
summary_haiku: Jorczak proposes a Collaborative Information Processing (CIP) model explaining how peer discussion facilitates learning through information divergence and convergence. Using information processing theory, the model demonstrates that groups benefit from diverse member perspectives triggering conceptual conflict, followed by convergent processes achieving shared understanding. The CIP framework unifies cognitive and social interaction theories, predicting that heterogeneous groups and divergent information exchange enhance collaborative learning outcomes.
evidence_span: title, abstract, theoretical framework
coding_notes: The article presents a theoretical model (CIP) grounded in information processing theory, predicting effects of group heterogeneity and divergence/convergence on learning. While the summary emphasizes theory and prediction rather than explicit empirical methodology, the framing suggests hypothesis-testing logic. Pedagogy coded as collaboration_scripts because the model emphasizes structured divergence–convergence processes; argumentation is secondary given the emphasis on conceptual conflict and shared understanding.

title: Comparing the effects of representational tools in collaborative and individual inquiry learning
authors: Bas Kolloffel & Tessa H. S. Eysink & Ton de Jong
summary_haiku: Collaborative learners significantly outperformed individual learners in combinatorics and probability inquiry learning, particularly on intuitive and situational knowledge. Using a pre-test/post-test design with 61 collaborative dyads and 95 individual students, three representational tool formats (conceptual, arithmetical, textual) were compared. Results showed collaboration's benefits persisted regardless of tool use, while individual learners benefited from externalization. Representational format did not directly enhance specific knowledge types as hypothesized, though approximately 50% adopted conceptual or textual tools versus only 20% using arithmetical formats.
evidence_span: methods (pre-test/post-test design, 61 dyads, 95 individuals, three tool formats) + findings (collaboration benefits, tool adoption rates)
coding_notes: Study employs a controlled comparison of collaborative vs. individual conditions with representational tool manipulation, fitting experimental design. Primary unit is dyad (collaborative learners) with secondary focus on individual outcomes. Inquiry learning in combinatorics/probability is the pedagogical context. Representational tools (conceptual, arithmetical, textual formats) function as shared workspaces for externalization.

title: A multimodal approach to coding discourse: Collaboration, distributed cognition, and geometric reasoning
authors: Michael A. Evans & Eliot Feenstra & Emily Ryon & David McNeill
summary_haiku: Researchers developed a multimodal coding framework to analyze distributed cognition in young children's collaborative problem-solving. Using speech, gesture, and gaze analysis, they tracked "coreferences"—shared references to objects, participants, and concepts—across three discourse levels. Applied to 7-8-year-olds solving tangrams physically and virtually, findings revealed increased meta-level communication and coalition formation in computer-supported settings, with dominant participants showing greater influence in virtual versus physical environments.
evidence_span: methods (multimodal coding framework, gaze/gesture/speech analysis) + findings (coreferences, meta-level communication, coalition formation)
coding_notes: Study employs fine-grained interaction analysis with multimodal sensors (eye-tracking, gesture) to examine distributed cognition across physical and virtual tangram-solving tasks. Primary unit is small groups of children; secondary focus on discourse traces (coreferences). No AI/LLM involvement detected.

title: Designing automated adaptive support to improve student helping behaviors in a peer tutoring activity
authors: Erin Walker & Nikol Rummel & Kenneth R. Koedinger
summary_haiku: Researchers used a four-phase iterative design process to develop adaptive support for peer tutoring in algebra. Through user needs analysis, system design, classroom experimentation, and qualitative case analysis, they found that adaptive assistance improved conceptual help quality and sentence classifier usage compared to fixed support, though learning gains were not significantly different. The study demonstrates how accountability-focused design principles can enhance collaborative help-giving behaviors.
evidence_span: methods (four-phase iterative design, classroom experimentation) + findings (adaptive vs. fixed support comparison, help quality metrics)
coding_notes: The study exemplifies design-based research with iterative cycles of design, implementation, and analysis in a naturalistic classroom setting. Adaptive support system functions as a collaboration script that structures peer tutoring help-giving; comparison of adaptive vs. fixed conditions provides quasi-experimental evidence. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

title: CSCL for intellectually disabled pupils: Stimulating interaction by using a floor control mechanism
authors: Ulrike Cress & Katrin Wodzicki & Martina Bientzle & Andreas Lingnau
summary_haiku: This study examined whether floor control mechanisms—restricting simultaneous actions in collaborative learning environments—improve interaction quality for intellectually disabled pupils. Twenty pupils completed a furniture-sorting task in pairs using tablet PCs, comparing floor control versus unrestricted conditions. Results showed floor control reduced relocations, decreased coordinative communication, and increased content-related discussion, particularly when pupils disagreed or faced difficult symbols, while producing slightly higher-quality collaborative outcomes.
evidence_span: methods (experimental design, floor control manipulation) + findings (interaction quality, coordinative vs. content-related communication)
coding_notes: Study uses a controlled comparison of floor control (structured constraint) versus unrestricted conditions, making it experimental. Floor control is a collaboration script mechanism embedded in tablet-based shared workspace. Analysis focuses on dyadic interaction quality and communication patterns, grounded in sociocultural and socio-cognitive perspectives on how structure scaffolds collaborative learning.

title: Student use of Facebook for organizing collaborative classroom activities
authors: Cliff Lampe & Donghee Yvette Wohn & Jessica Vitak & Nicole B. Ellison & Rick Wash
summary_haiku: Two survey studies examined how undergraduate students repurpose Facebook for classroom organizing. Study 1 (N=302) found that Facebook intensity and willingness to contact instructors predicted collaboration propensity. Study 2 (N=214) revealed two distinct collaboration types: positive (instructor-approved) and negative (unapproved), with different predictors including self-efficacy and relational communication strategies, suggesting how students use Facebook matters more than frequency.
evidence_span: methods (two survey studies) + findings (predictors of collaboration types)
coding_notes: Survey-based studies report frequencies and correlations (e.g., Facebook intensity predicting collaboration propensity), with secondary inferential testing. Facebook repurposing for classroom organizing reflects asynchronous social media use; instructor approval suggests pedagogical structure. Sociocultural framing emphasizes social mediation of learning through peer networks.

title: Identity presence and knowledge building: Joint emergence in online learning environments?
authors: Fengfeng Ke & Alicia F. Chavez & Pei-Ni L. Causarano & Antonio Causarano
summary_haiku: This mixed-method study examined identity presence in seven online courses and its relationship to knowledge building. Using discourse analysis of 1,817 discussion posts, researchers found that posts expressing personal experiences, cultural perspectives, and age-related views elicited significantly more responses and correlated with knowledge-sharing interactions. However, identity presence did not significantly predict higher-level collaborative knowledge construction, suggesting online learners prioritize self-expression over negotiating shared understanding.
evidence_span: methods (discourse analysis of 1,817 posts across seven courses) + findings (correlation of identity presence with knowledge-sharing; non-significance for collaborative knowledge construction)
coding_notes: Study explicitly uses discourse analysis of discussion posts as primary method, combined with quantitative correlation analysis, making it mixed-methods. Primary unit is the post/artifact and course cohort. Knowledge building theory frames the inquiry into whether identity presence supports collective knowledge advancement.

title: Agent-based dynamic support for learning from collaborative brainstorming in scientific inquiry
authors: Hao-Chuan Wang & Carolyn P. Rose & Chun-Yen Chang
summary_haiku: This study examines learning during collaborative brainstorming through two controlled experiments manipulating individual versus pair work and system support. Results reveal that while pair brainstorming produces process losses in idea generation, it enhances multi-perspective learning. The VIBRANT agent's automatic feedback improves connection-based learning. An enhanced version in study two shows promise for mitigating productivity losses associated with collaborative work.
evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (two controlled experiments), findings (pair vs. individual, VIBRANT agent feedback effects)
coding_notes: Study uses controlled experiments comparing individual and pair brainstorming with/without agent support (VIBRANT), measuring learning outcomes and idea generation. Agent provides automatic feedback to scaffold connection-based learning. AI involvement coded as non-LLM (rule-based agent) with secondary feedback component; LLM classification uncertain but agent appears to use heuristic rules rather than neural language models typical of 2011.

title: Scaffolding collaborative technical writing with procedural facilitation and synchronous discussion
authors: Shiou-Wen Yeh & Jia-Jiunn Lo & Jeng-Jia Huang
summary_haiku: Researchers developed Process-Writing Wizard, a computer-supported system combining procedural scaffolding and synchronous chat to facilitate collaborative technical writing among EFL students. An experimental study with 48 students compared the system against standard chat. Results showed experimental group students demonstrated significantly higher perceived usefulness, positive attitudes, and stronger intention to reuse the system. Their articles exhibited superior content and organization quality, and synchronous discussions focused more on article-related interactions rather than social exchanges.
evidence_span: methods (experimental design, 48 students, two conditions) + findings (perceived usefulness, article quality, chat interaction patterns)
coding_notes: Study employs a controlled comparison of two conditions (Process-Writing Wizard vs. standard chat), making it experimental. Procedural scaffolding and synchronous discussion are core technologies. Content analysis of articles and chat interactions supports the secondary methodology and unit-of-analysis coding.

title: Are two heads always better than one? Differential effects of collaboration on students’ computer-supported learning in mathematics
authors: Dejana Mullins & Nikol Rummel & Hans Spada
summary_haiku: Collaboration's effectiveness in mathematics learning depends on instructional material type. This experimental study compared individual versus collaborative learning with conceptual and procedural algebra instruction in a computer-supported environment. Results showed collaboration enhanced conceptual knowledge acquisition through mutual elaboration, but hindered procedural skill development due to task distribution and reduced practice opportunities.
evidence_span: methods (experimental design comparing individual vs. collaborative conditions) + findings (differential effects on conceptual vs. procedural knowledge)
coding_notes: Study uses controlled comparison of collaboration vs. individual conditions with inferential testing of learning outcomes. Primary focus is dyadic collaboration in computer-supported algebra learning, with secondary attention to individual learner outcomes. Socio-cognitive theory (collaborative conflict and explanation) combined with sociocultural framing of computer-mediated interaction.

title: Analyzing temporal patterns of knowledge construction in a role-based online discussion
authors: Alyssa Friend Wise
summary_haiku: This study analyzed temporal patterns of knowledge construction in role-based online discussions using content analysis and statistical discourse analysis. Examining 252 posts from 21 university students, researchers identified pivotal posts that divided discussions into distinct segments. Results showed most discussions progressed from lower to higher knowledge construction phases, with mid-discussion summaries by Synthesizer and Wrapper roles acting as pivotal posts that elevated subsequent discussion quality, supporting the progressive nature of collaborative knowledge construction.
evidence_span: methods (content analysis, statistical discourse analysis) + findings (pivotal posts, knowledge construction phases, temporal progression)
coding_notes: Study uses systematic coding of discussion posts to identify knowledge construction phases and pivotal posts; temporal sequence analysis reveals progression patterns. Role-based scripting (Synthesizer, Wrapper) is the pedagogical structure enabling collaborative knowledge advancement.

title: The impact of scripted roles on online collaborative learning processes
authors: Francesca Pozzi
summary_haiku: This pilot study examined how scripted "opinion-centered" roles impact online collaborative learning in an asynchronous text-based environment. Using content analysis of 209 student messages and post-activity questionnaires, researchers evaluated four dimensions: participative, social, cognitive, and teaching. Results showed roles effectively fostered group cohesion and knowledge building, though metacognition remained underdeveloped. Students' perceptions largely aligned with message analysis, indicating awareness of the collaborative process.
evidence_span: methods + findings
coding_notes: Study uses systematic coding of 209 messages (content analysis) combined with descriptive statistics and questionnaire data. Scripted roles are the core pedagogical intervention; asynchronous text-based environment is the technology. Sociocultural framing evident in focus on group cohesion and collaborative knowledge building.

title: Interactive tabletops in education
authors: Pierre Dillenbourg
summary_haiku: Interactive tabletops support co-located collaborative learning through hands-on manipulation of objects, conveying socio-constructivist pedagogical approaches. This analytical framework examines 33 design considerations across four levels: user-system interaction, teamwork dynamics, classroom orchestration, and socio-cultural contexts. The authors argue that tabletops' educational effectiveness depends on thoughtful design addressing these specific affordances rather than inherent technological properties.
evidence_span: title, abstract, framework description
coding_notes: This is a design-focused analytical framework paper rather than an empirical study with primary data collection. Coded as ethnographic_case_study as a proxy for qualitative design analysis; could also fit design_based_research. The framework explicitly addresses tabletop affordances for co-located collaboration and socio-constructivist pedagogy across multiple analytical levels.

title: Multi-touch tables and the relationship with collaborative classroom pedagogies: A synthetic review
authors: Steven E. Higgins & Emma Mercier & Elizabeth Burd & Andrew Hatch
summary_haiku: Multi-touch tables offer significant potential for supporting collaborative classroom learning through their design features. This synthetic review proposes a typology categorizing hardware characteristics—surface geometry and display type, touch sensing capabilities, and connectivity—to analyze how technical affordances align with pedagogical goals. Evidence suggests horizontal multi-touch surfaces enable more equitable participation and task-focused interaction than traditional single-touch technologies, though text entry limitations and teacher orchestration challenges require further investigation.
evidence_span: title, abstract, and review scope
coding_notes: This is a synthetic/literature review that systematically categorizes and analyzes hardware affordances and pedagogical alignment of multi-touch tables. The primary methodology is content analysis of existing studies and design features; secondary descriptive statistics likely summarize findings across reviewed studies. The unit of analysis is primarily the technological artifact and its interaction traces, with classroom cohorts as the learning context. Theory is sociocultural (learning through collaborative interaction) and distributed cognition (cognition spread across people and tangible interface).

title: Interfering and resolving: How tabletop interaction facilitates co-construction of argumentative knowledge
authors: Taciana Pontual Falcao & Sara Price
summary_haiku: Peer interference in shared tabletop interfaces can productively support argumentative knowledge co-construction during exploratory science learning. Analyzing 43 students aged 11-14 interacting with a tangible light-behavior simulation, researchers applied Weinberger and Fischer's consensus-building framework to interference episodes. Integration-oriented consensus building—where students reflected on and incorporated peers' contributions—consistently produced productive learning, while conflict-oriented approaches typically yielded counter-productive outcomes.
evidence_span: methods (interaction coding, consensus-building framework) + findings (interference episodes, learning outcomes)
coding_notes: Study employs micro-analytic coding of collaborative episodes (interaction_analysis) combined with systematic categorization of consensus-building strategies (content_analysis). Tabletop tangible interface is the primary technology enabling co-construction; analysis focuses on dyadic/small-group argumentative knowledge building through peer interference and resolution.

title: Collaboration within large groups in the classroom
authors: Eyal Szewkis & Miguel Nussbaum & Tal Rosen & Jose Abalos & Fernanda Denardin & Daniela Caballero & Arturo Tagle & Cristian Alcoholado
summary_haiku: This study investigates large-group classroom collaboration using Single Display Groupware with multiple mice and minimal hardware. Through an experimental design comparing 42 students using the system for 40% of class time against 32 control students, researchers found that "silent collaboration"—a negotiation mechanism enabling object exchanges—effectively facilitated synchronous learning in Spanish language tasks. Results demonstrated significant learning gains and successful achievement of collaborative conditions, suggesting this low-cost approach enables effective large-group computer-supported collaborative learning.
evidence_span: methods (experimental design, 42 vs 32 students) + findings (learning gains, silent collaboration mechanism)
coding_notes: Study employs controlled comparison of treatment (SDG with multiple mice) vs control group, measuring learning outcomes in Spanish language tasks. 'Silent collaboration' is a structured negotiation mechanism, aligning with collaboration scripts pedagogy. Single Display Groupware is a shared workspace tool enabling synchronous co-editing/interaction.

title: Guided reciprocal questioning to support children’s collaborative storytelling
authors: Giulia Gelmini-Hornsby & Shaaron Ainsworth
summary_haiku: Guided Reciprocal Peer Questioning (GRPQ) scripts significantly enhance children's collaborative storytelling through increased interactive discussion. Using a within-subjects design with 36 six-to-seven-year-olds creating stories with KidPad, the study found that question prompts promoted longer, more evaluatively rich, and more coherent stories. Benefits largely persisted after scaffold withdrawal, suggesting children internalized the questioning approach and can apply it independently.
evidence_span: methods (within-subjects design, 36 children, KidPad) + findings (question prompts, story quality, persistence)
coding_notes: Within-subjects design with scaffold withdrawal condition is quasi-experimental. GRPQ is a collaboration script using reciprocal questioning prompts. KidPad is a shared digital canvas for co-authoring stories. Analysis includes both interaction patterns (discourse richness) and artifact quality (story coherence).

title: Scaffolding of small groups’ metacognitive activities with an avatar
authors: Inge Molenaar & Ming Ming Chiu & Peter Sleegers & Carla van Boxtel
summary_haiku: Avatar-based metacognitive scaffolding in small group learning environments influences student knowledge acquisition through mediation by metacognitive activities. Multivariate multilevel analysis of 51,339 conversation turns from 54 elementary students revealed that problematizing scaffolds (eliciting student explanations) produced greater domain knowledge than structuring scaffolds (providing examples), with metacognitive activities mediating these effects. Both scaffold types enhanced metacognitive knowledge primarily through increased metacognitive engagement.
evidence_span: methods (multivariate multilevel analysis of 51,339 conversation turns), findings (scaffold types and metacognitive mediation effects)
coding_notes: Study uses avatar-based scaffolding (collaboration scripting tool) to structure metacognitive activities in small groups. Multilevel modeling explicitly analyzes nested conversation turns within students; interaction analysis evident in coding of 51,339 turns. Sociocultural framing (mediation, scaffolding) with socio-cognitive elements (explanation-driven learning).

title: Building a community among teachers, researchers and university students. A blended approach to training
authors: Donatella Cesareni & Francesca Martini & Ilaria Mancini
summary_haiku: # Summary This case study examined a blended learning community of 45 Italian teachers, researchers, and university students participating in the ITCOLE project. Using qualitative analysis of face-to-face and online interactions, researchers found that expert teachers assumed central roles while novice teachers engaged in legitimate peripheral participation, gradually becoming more competent community members. Teachers recognized CSCL's innovative potential for student motivation and collaborative knowledge building, though they identified challenges including technical infrastructure limitations and heavy workload demands.
evidence_span: summary describes qualitative analysis of face-to-face and online interactions; legitimate peripheral participation and community roles evident
coding_notes: Case study of a bounded blended learning community with qualitative analysis of interactions across modalities. Lave & Wenger's LPP framework and community-of-practice lens are central; secondary coding includes social network analysis (expert/novice roles) and content analysis of discourse. No AI/LLM involvement in 2011 study.

title: Making rounds: The routine work of the teacher during collaborative learning with computers
authors: Christian Greiffenhagen
summary_haiku: This ethnomethodological study analyzes teacher interventions during collaborative computer-based learning using video recordings of English lessons with storyboarding software. Through detailed conversation analysis of naturally occurring classroom interactions, the author identifies five types of teacher practices: ratifying pupil work, reminding pupils of task requirements, making suggestions for improvement, maintaining classroom control, and making whole-class announcements. The analysis reveals that classroom management and pedagogy are intertwined rather than separate, and tensions between teacher and pupil perspectives are collaborative rather than antagonistic.
evidence_span: methods (video ethnomethodology, conversation analysis) + findings (five teacher intervention types)
coding_notes: Ethnomethodological approach with detailed conversation analysis of moment-by-moment teacher moves during collaborative computer-based learning. Primary focus is teacher facilitation practices and their interplay with classroom management; secondary attention to small-group dynamics. Storyboarding software is a shared workspace tool.

title: How gamers manage aggression: Situating skills in collaborative computer games
authors: Ulrika Bennerstedt & Jonas Ivarsson & Jonas Linderoth
summary_haiku: Using ethnomethodological analysis of boss encounters in a massively multiplayer online game, this study examines skills gamers develop during collaborative gameplay involving portrayed aggression. The researchers found that "aggression" and "collaboration" manifest as highly specialized, game-specific practices—particularly aggro management—rather than transferable general skills. The analysis challenges assumptions underlying both positive and negative gaming effects research, arguing that claims about behavioral transfer require explicit theoretical justification and risk oversimplification.
evidence_span: methods (ethnomethodological analysis of boss encounters) + findings (aggro management as specialized practice)
coding_notes: Study uses fine-grained interaction analysis of collaborative gameplay episodes (boss encounters in MMO), grounded in ethnomethodological approach. Primary unit is small groups managing coordinated aggression; secondary focus on game-specific discourse/practices as artifacts. Pedagogy reflects implicit collaboration scripts (role-based aggro management) and peer regulation within gameplay.

title: The multivoicedness of game play: Exploring the unfolding of a student’s learning trajectory in a gaming context at school
authors: Kenneth Silseth
summary_haiku: This qualitative case study examines how classroom interactions facilitate a student's learning trajectory while playing the educational game Global Conflicts: Palestine. Using sociocultural and dialogic analysis of video-recorded gameplay and discussions, the research demonstrates that computer games become learning resources through collaborative meaning-making. The teacher's role in orchestrating dialogic spaces where multiple perspectives "inter-animate" each other proved crucial for developing nuanced understanding of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict's complexity.
evidence_span: methods (video-recorded gameplay and discussions, qualitative case study) + findings (learning trajectory, dialogic meaning-making)
coding_notes: The study employs fine-grained interaction and discourse analysis of video-recorded classroom episodes to trace one student's learning trajectory. While the game is the artifact under study, the primary analytical focus is on the moment-by-moment unfolding of collaborative dialogue and teacher orchestration, characteristic of interaction analysis. Dialogic theory (Bakhtin's multi-voicedness) and sociocultural theory (Vygotsky) are explicitly foregrounded.

title: Personal and shared experiences as resources for meaning making in a philosophy of science course
authors: Maarit Arvaja
