coding_notes: Video analysis of moment-by-moment collaborative episodes with attention to gestures, physical objects, and digital tools (GoogleEarth) indicates interaction analysis as primary. Distributed cognition and sociocultural framing emphasize imagination as socially, embodily, and materially distributed across people and artifacts. Secondary methods include multimodal observation (gestures, objects) and ethnographic case-study design of small-group problem-solving.

title: Socio-cognitive openness in online knowledge building discourse: does openness keep conversations going?
authors: Frank P. C. M. de Jong & Jan van Aalst & Natascha de Hoog & Hennie van Heijst & Paul A. Kirschner
summary_haiku: This study analyzes socio-cognitive openness in online knowledge-building discourse among Master's students using a framework with four social and four cognitive components. Analyzing 638 Knowledge Forum contributions, researchers found moderate openness levels with higher social than cognitive openness. Cognitive openness indicators—particularly elaboration, justification, and inviting response—positively predicted follow-up contributions, while social openness showed no significant relationship. Expressing uncertainty emerged as key to sustaining knowledge-building conversations.
evidence_span: methods (framework, 638 contributions coded), findings (openness levels, predictive relationships)
coding_notes: Study systematically codes Knowledge Forum posts using a socio-cognitive openness framework, then uses inferential statistics (regression) to predict follow-up contributions. Primary focus is content analysis of discourse artifacts; secondary methods include statistical inference and discourse-level interpretation aligned with knowledge-building theory.

title: Conceptualizing the designs of authentic
authors: Yotam Hod & Ornit Sagy
summary_haiku: This study synthesizes 25 years of CSCL research using constant-comparative analysis to clarify authentic learning design. The authors identify three cultures—current, authentic, and intended—operating in authentic learning environments and distinguish between simulation approaches (classroom-based enculturation) and hybrid approaches (direct practitioner interaction). A coding scheme analyzing participants, settings, time, computer support, and collaboration reveals that timeframe most clearly differentiates approaches, offering CSCL designers a refined conceptual framework and visualization tool for understanding authentic learning environment variations.
evidence_span: methods (constant-comparative analysis, coding scheme) + findings (three cultures framework, simulation vs. hybrid distinction)
coding_notes: This is a systematic literature review synthesizing 25 years of CSCL research using constant-comparative analysis and a structured coding scheme to analyze design dimensions (participants, settings, time, computer support, collaboration). Primary methodology is content_analysis because the authors systematically code and categorize existing CSCL studies. Unit of analysis is artifact_discourse_trace because the primary objects analyzed are research publications and their design descriptions. Theory is communities_of_practice because the framework emphasizes authentic participation in practitioner communities; activity_theory is secondary given the focus on contradictions between intended and actual cultures.

title: Towards a micro-ecological approach to CSCL
authors: Marcela Borge
summary_haiku: # Summary Current CSCL theories prioritize single-level analysis, limiting understanding of complex orchestration processes. This paper proposes a micro-ecological framework analyzing interactions across individual, group, and classroom levels simultaneously. Through a design club case study, the authors identify "transecological disruptions"—critical moments where actions at one level propagate across levels—demonstrating how this approach reveals orchestration complexity and learning opportunities that traditional single-level analyses miss.
evidence_span: abstract, summary, and theoretical framing
coding_notes: The paper proposes a micro-ecological framework analyzing simultaneous interactions across individual, group, and classroom levels, making cross-level multilevel analysis the primary unit. Activity theory and distributed cognition align with the focus on orchestration processes and transecological disruptions propagating across system levels. Ethnographic case study of a design club is the primary methodology, with interaction analysis supporting the micro-level examination of critical moments.

title: Learners’ agency and CSCL technologies: towards an emancipatory perspective
authors: future of CSCL
summary_haiku: This conceptual article argues that CSCL should adopt an emancipatory perspective prioritizing learners' agency over technology-imposed constraints. Tchounikine proposes that learners should be empowered to select, adapt, and interoperate software applications while receiving informed feedback. The analysis identifies key challenges: enabling technology choice, supporting customization, and providing transparent information—requiring fundamental reconceptualization of CSCL technologies as services rather than fixed applications.
evidence_span: title, abstract, conceptual framing
coding_notes: This is a conceptual/theoretical position paper rather than an empirical study, so methodology and unit of analysis do not apply in traditional sense. The work prioritizes learners' agency and emancipatory perspective (critical_pragmatic lens) within a sociocultural framework, but does not report empirical data collection or analysis. Technology is discussed abstractly as a design principle rather than a specific tool.

title: Deliberative emotional talk
authors: Benzi Slakmon & Baruch B. Schwarz
summary_haiku: This study demonstrates that high-quality deliberative discussions about controversial issues can integrate strong emotions with argumentative rigor. Using design-based research, the authors developed the Hot Discussions Platform (HDP), a CSCL tool enabling teachers to design, moderate, and reflect on emotionally-engaged discussions. Through a 30-hour professional development course with 25 teachers, analysis revealed teachers recognize emotions as essential to democratic education and develop sophisticated moderation practices balancing authentic expression with critical thinking standards, establishing proof-of-concept for "deliberative emotional talk."
evidence_span: methods, findings, design iteration
coding_notes: Design-based research iteratively develops and studies the Hot Discussions Platform (HDP) with teachers as primary unit of analysis; focus on teacher moderation practices and deliberative emotional talk reflects dialogic and critical-pragmatic orientations. Secondary methods include content analysis of discussion artifacts and ethnographic observation of teacher learning during PD.

title: Real-time orchestrational technologies in
authors: Camillia Matuk & Michael Tissenbaum
summary_haiku: Real-time dashboards in computer-supported collaborative learning environments enable teachers to monitor student progress and provide timely, targeted guidance during complex collaborative activities. This special issue examines five empirical studies investigating how real-time data visualization supports classroom orchestration, finding that effective designs partner with teachers rather than replace their functions, balance automated support with teacher autonomy, and require participatory design involving educators throughout development.
evidence_span: title, abstract, and summary describing real-time dashboards, teacher monitoring, classroom orchestration, and participatory design
coding_notes: This is a special issue editorial/overview examining five empirical studies on real-time orchestrational dashboards. The primary focus is on teacher awareness and decision-making during collaborative learning, supported by data visualization tools. Design-based research is inferred from the emphasis on iterative, participatory design involving educators; learning analytics is secondary because trace data visualization is central to the intervention.

title: What information should CSCL teacher dashboards provide to help teachers interpret CSCL situations?
authors: Anouschka van Leeuwen & Nikol Rummel & Tamara van Gog
summary_haiku: Teachers struggle to interpret collaborative learning situations from dashboards. This experimental study (n=53) compared three dashboard types—mirroring, alerting, and advising—examining how different support levels affect teachers' detection and interpretation of student collaboration problems in fraction tasks. Results showed dashboard type did not influence detection speed or accuracy, but advising dashboards significantly improved interpretation depth, with teachers adopting more analytical stances toward situations.
evidence_span: methods (experimental design, n=53, three dashboard conditions) + findings (detection speed/accuracy, interpretation depth)
coding_notes: Study is a controlled experiment manipulating dashboard design (mirroring, alerting, advising) to examine teacher interpretation of CSCL situations. Primary focus is teacher awareness and decision-making supported by visualization tools; secondary analysis likely involved coding teacher responses or interpretations (content analysis). No AI/LLM involvement detected.

title: Correction to: A handheld classroom dashboard: teachers’ perspectives on the use of real-time collaborative learning analytics
authors: Roberto Martinez-Maldonado
summary_haiku: This correction notice addresses duplicate images in the original article examining teachers' perspectives on a handheld classroom dashboard for real-time collaborative learning analytics. The correction republishes the correct versions of Figures 4 and 6, which display visualizations of group task progress, individual participation, and real-time feedback on learning design enactment.
evidence_span: title and correction notice only
coding_notes: This is a correction notice, not a research article. Only the technology (handheld classroom dashboard for real-time analytics) can be reliably identified from the title and excerpt. Methodology, unit of analysis, pedagogy, and theory cannot be determined from a correction notice alone; the original article would be needed for full coding.

title: Guiding collaborative revision of science explanations
authors: Libby Gerard & Ady Kidron
summary_haiku: Combining automated explanation scoring with teacher guidance in a computer-supported collaborative learning environment, this study examined how one sixth-grade teacher customized adaptive feedback to guide 98 student pairs in revising science explanations about plate tectonics. Analysis of classroom interactions revealed five distinct teacher guidance strategies that leveraged automated scores to personalize support. Results showed nearly all pairs engaged in meaningful revision, with significant improvements in explanation quality and individual posttest gains, demonstrating how teacher-computer partnerships can effectively promote collaborative knowledge integration.
evidence_span: methods, results, discussion
coding_notes: Study combines quantitative outcome measures (posttest gains, revision quality) with qualitative interaction analysis of teacher guidance strategies. Automated explanation scoring is rule-based AI (not LLM), but the teacher uses scores to provide adaptive feedback. Primary unit is student pairs revising collaboratively; teacher facilitation is secondary analytical focus.

title: Supporting classroom orchestration with real-time feedback: A role for teacher dashboards and real-time agents
authors: Mike Tissenbaum & Jim Slotta
summary_haiku: This design-based research study investigates how real-time software agents and teacher dashboards support orchestration of complex collaborative physics inquiry in high school classrooms. Using the Knowledge Community and Inquiry model, researchers developed SAIL Smart Space technology with four agent types to dynamically manage student grouping, material allocation, and teacher notifications. Results demonstrate that the tablet-based orchestration system successfully reduced teacher workload while enabling timely interventions that significantly improved student problem-solving outcomes.
evidence_span: title, abstract, methods, findings
coding_notes: Design-based research iteratively develops and studies SAIL Smart Space with rule-based software agents (not LLMs) managing grouping and notifications. Teacher dashboards and agents are central to orchestration support in a physics inquiry classroom. Sociocultural framing emphasizes mediation of collaborative learning through technology and teacher awareness.

title: It is not either or: An initial investigation into combining collaborative and individual learning using an ITS
authors: Nikol Rummel & Vincent Aleven & Jennifer K. Olsen
summary_haiku: This study compared combined collaborative-individual learning to either approach alone using an intelligent tutoring system for fractions with 382 elementary students. Results showed the combined condition produced higher learning gains than individual or collaborative-only conditions, particularly for fourth graders. Process data revealed combined-condition students made fewer errors and requested fewer hints, while reporting greater situational interest in the activity.
evidence_span: methods (experimental design, 382 students, three conditions) + findings (learning gains, process data, error rates, hint requests, situational interest)
coding_notes: Study uses a controlled comparison of three conditions (combined collaborative-individual, collaborative-only, individual-only) with an ITS for fractions. Primary unit is individual learner outcomes (learning gains, errors, hints, interest), though dyads are involved in the collaborative conditions. The ITS is a shared workspace supporting both collaborative and individual problem-solving phases.

title: A handheld classroom dashboard: Teachers’ perspectives on the use of real-time collaborative learning analytics
authors: Roberto Martinez-Maldonado
summary_haiku: This longitudinal study examined four teachers' perspectives on using a real-time analytics dashboard during 72 classroom sessions over ten weeks in a multi-tabletop collaborative learning environment. The handheld dashboard displayed group participation, task progress, script enactment, and automatically detected misconceptions. Through semi-structured interviews, teachers reported that visualizations enhanced awareness and decision-making, though they identified tensions regarding data incompleteness, immediate versus delayed feedback, orchestration load, and device portability, highlighting critical design considerations for effective CSCL classroom analytics tools.
evidence_span: methods (longitudinal study, semi-structured interviews, 72 sessions), findings (teacher perspectives on dashboard visualizations, orchestration tensions)
coding_notes: Study centers on real-time learning analytics dashboard supporting teacher awareness and orchestration in tabletop collaborative environments. Automatic misconception detection suggests ML/AI-based analytics, but no explicit LLM involvement; coded as learning_analytics with awareness_dashboard as primary technology. Teacher facilitation is the primary analytical lens, though classroom cohort is also examined.

title: Capturing the dynamic and cyclical nature of regulation: Methodological Progress in understanding socially shared regulation in learning
authors: Hanna Jarvenoja
summary_haiku: This review examines methodological progress in researching socially shared regulation (SSRL) of learning in collaborative and computer-supported collaborative learning contexts. The authors identify three key challenges: capturing regulation's cyclical, temporal nature; understanding how self-regulation, co-regulation, and SSRL jointly contribute to learning; and studying SSRL in authentic contexts. They advocate for multimodal data collection methods, technological tools for prompting regulation, and analyzing learning challenges as triggers for regulatory processes.
evidence_span: abstract, introduction, and methodological discussion sections
coding_notes: This is a methodological review article examining SSRL research rather than an empirical study. The primary methodology reflects the mixed-methods nature of studies reviewed and the emphasis on capturing temporal, cyclical regulation through multimodal data. Secondary units reflect the nested individual-group-class dynamics central to SSRL theory.

title: Are we together or not? The temporal interplay of monitoring, physiological arousal and physiological synchrony during a collaborative exam
authors: Jonna Malmberg & Eetu Haataja & Tapio Seppanen & Sanna Jarvela
summary_haiku: This study examined metacognitive monitoring during collaborative exams using video analysis and physiological sensors measuring electrodermal activity. Results showed all group members contributed to monitoring, with monitoring frequency significantly correlating with physiological arousal peaks. Physiological synchrony occurred in groups experiencing task difficulties, suggesting it may indicate meaningful collaborative learning events requiring intervention.
evidence_span: methods (video analysis, physiological sensors) + findings (monitoring frequency, arousal peaks, synchrony patterns)
coding_notes: Study combines micro-analytic video coding of monitoring behaviors with physiological sensor data (electrodermal activity) to examine temporal dynamics in collaborative groups. Primary focus is interaction analysis of moment-by-moment metacognitive monitoring; physiological sensors are secondary methodological tool. Sociocultural framing emphasizes collaborative regulation and shared awareness during joint problem-solving.

title: Cohesion in online environments
authors: Maria Altebarmakian & Richard Alterman
summary_haiku: Online group cohesion emerges from students' engagement choices in asynchronous collaboration. This case study analyzed 29 students completing design assignments through a custom platform, measuring cohesion via behavioral engagement, interactivity, and cognitive engagement. Results show students prioritized thoughtful commenting over interactive dialogue, achieving moderate cohesion sufficient for reflective meaning-making but limited direct negotiation of ideas.
evidence_span: methods (case study design, cohesion measurement via behavioral/cognitive engagement coding) + findings (engagement patterns, commenting vs. dialogue)
coding_notes: Study employs systematic coding of student engagement behaviors (behavioral, interactivity, cognitive dimensions) in asynchronous platform interactions, characteristic of content analysis. Secondary methodology includes descriptive statistics on cohesion measures. Peer review/feedback is primary pedagogy given emphasis on commenting; inquiry-based design assignments are secondary. Asynchronous forum is primary technology; shared workspace (custom platform for collaborative design) is secondary.

title: Good for learning, bad for motivation? A meta-analysis on the effects of computer-supported collaboration scripts
authors: Anika Radkowitsch & Freydis Vogel & Frank Fischer
summary_haiku: This meta-analysis of 53 studies examined computer-supported collaboration scripts' effects on learner outcomes. Results showed scripts produced non-significant positive effects on motivation, small positive effects on domain learning, and medium positive effects on collaboration skills. Contrary to widespread criticism, scripts did not undermine motivation. However, combining multiple collaborative activity prompts generally reduced effectiveness compared to single-activity scripts, suggesting simpler designs may be more beneficial for learning.
evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (meta-analysis of 53 studies), findings (effect sizes on motivation, learning, collaboration skills)
coding_notes: Meta-analysis synthesizes quantitative effect sizes across multiple studies using inferential statistics (meta-regression, heterogeneity testing). Primary unit is the study/intervention artifact (collaboration scripts); secondary is cross-level because meta-analyses aggregate individual and group outcomes. Pedagogy centers on collaboration scripts; theory draws on socio-cognitive (explanation, conflict) and sociocultural (mediated activity) frameworks implicit in script design.

title: Distributed spatial Sensemaking on the augmented reality sandbox
authors: Yotam Hod & Daniel Twersky
summary_haiku: This study uses Interaction Analysis to examine how small collaborative groups engage in distributed spatial sensemaking while using an Augmented Reality Sandbox for topographical learning. Findings reveal that AR features (contour lines, water simulations) coordinated with a 2D monitor representation enable groups to rapidly develop intrinsic-dynamic spatial thinking, facilitate quick trouble-repair sequences, and support divergent-to-convergent turn-taking patterns essential for advancing spatial understanding.
evidence_span: title, abstract, methodology description
coding_notes: Study explicitly employs Interaction Analysis of moment-by-moment collaborative episodes on an AR tangible interface. Distributed cognition is the primary theoretical lens given emphasis on spatial sensemaking spread across group members, the AR artifact, and the 2D monitor representation. Sociocultural framing is secondary (collaborative learning context).

title: Learning in embodied activity framework: a sociocultural framework for embodied cognition
authors: Joshua A. Danish & Noel Enyedy & Asmalina Saleh & Megan Humburg
summary_haiku: This paper proposes the Learning in Embodied Activity Framework (LEAF), which synthesizes individual and sociocultural theories to explain how bodies support collaborative learning. Using Cultural Historical Activity Theory, the authors analyze data from the Science through Technology Enhanced Play project, where first and second-grade students used mixed-reality simulations to learn about particle behavior and states of matter. LEAF extends embodied cognition research by explicitly examining how individual and collective embodied actions, mediated by tools, rules, community, and division of labor, jointly shape learning in collaborative contexts.
evidence_span: title, abstract, framework description, methods (mixed-reality simulations with first/second-grade students)
coding_notes: LEAF explicitly grounds analysis in Cultural Historical Activity Theory (Engeström), examining embodied collaborative learning in a naturalistic classroom setting with iterative design of mixed-reality simulations. The focus on how bodies, tools, and social structures jointly mediate learning aligns with activity theory and distributed cognition; interaction analysis of embodied actions is central to the framework.

title: Unpacking the relationship between existing and new measures of physiological synchrony and collaborative learning: a mixed methods study
authors: Bertrand Schneider
summary_haiku: This mixed-methods study examined how electrodermal activity (EDA) measures physiological synchrony in collaborative learning. Forty-two dyads programmed robots while wearing EDA sensors. Pearson's correlation and directional agreement showed modest associations with learning gains and collaboration quality. Qualitative analysis of high and low-performing groups revealed that synchrony peaks during external events, oscillates during collaboration, and drops during independent work. A novel measure—cycles between low and high synchrony—strongly correlated with collaboration quality and learning outcomes, suggesting it captures distinct collaborative dynamics.
evidence_span: methods, results, discussion
coding_notes: Study combines quantitative physiological sensor data (EDA) with qualitative interaction analysis of dyadic robot-programming tasks. The novel synchrony measure (cycles between low/high states) represents a methodological contribution bridging quantitative and qualitative understanding of collaborative dynamics.

title: Capturing the participation and social dimensions of
authors: Mohammed Saqr & Olga Viberg & Henriikka Vartiainen
summary_haiku: This study validates social network analysis centrality measures for analyzing computer-supported collaborative learning. Using data from 12 university courses with 598 students, researchers examined how different network configurations (multigraph, simplified, weighted) affect the reproducibility of centrality measures as indicators of student performance. Results show multigraph configuration produces the most consistent and robust measures, with degree centralities reliably indicating participation and eigenvector centrality consistently reflecting social dimensions across configurations.
evidence_span: methods, results, validation focus
coding_notes: Study is methodological validation of SNA centrality measures applied to CSCL data across 12 courses (n=598). Primary focus is on network configuration effects on reproducibility of centrality indices as proxies for participation and social position; no specific pedagogical intervention or technology platform is the focus. Distributed cognition and sociocultural framing implicit in treating collaboration as network-embedded social activity.

title: Does collaborative learning design align with enactment? An innovative method of evaluating the alignment in the CSCL context
authors: Lanqin Zheng & Panpan Cui
summary_haiku: This study proposes design-centered research (DCR), a novel quantitative methodology for evaluating alignment between collaborative learning designs and their actual enactment. Using three indicators—activated knowledge range, knowledge-building degree, and interactive approach—plus interaction path graphs, researchers analyzed 40 groups across two iterations. Results show significant alignment improvements in round two after design optimization, with corresponding gains in group performance, demonstrating that data-driven design refinement enhances collaborative learning effectiveness.
evidence_span: title, abstract, methods, findings
coding_notes: Study explicitly frames itself as design-centered research with iterative refinement across two rounds. Primary unit is 40 groups analyzed via interaction path graphs and three quantitative indicators (activated knowledge range, knowledge-building degree, interactive approach). Methodology combines design iteration with descriptive statistics and interaction-level analysis of collaborative traces.

title: Talking about group (but not individual) process aids group performance
authors: Noel Capon & Hueiyi Lai & Deanna Kuhn
summary_haiku: # Summary This study examined how group discourse relates to collaborative problem-solving performance. Graduate business students worked in small groups through a computer-supported marketing simulation over eight sessions. Discourse analysis revealed that groups discussing their collective process (Meta-group talk) achieved superior outcomes, while talk focused on individual perspectives (Meta-self talk) correlated negatively with performance. Meta-group discourse included understanding others, defining group position, planning, and evaluating—functions that facilitate coordinated action essential for effective collaboration.
evidence_span: methods (discourse analysis coding scheme) + findings (correlation of meta-group vs meta-self talk with performance)
coding_notes: Study uses systematic discourse coding to categorize group talk (meta-group vs meta-self) and correlates these categories with performance outcomes. Primary focus is on linguistic/rhetorical analysis of collaborative episodes, with secondary quantitative correlation analysis. Sociocultural framing emphasizes how collective reflection on group process mediates collaborative problem-solving.

title: Regulating self-organized collaborative learning: the importance of homogeneous problem perception, immediacy and intensity of strategy use
authors: Martin Greisel & Markus Dresel & Ingo Kollar & Nadine Melzner
summary_haiku: Self-organized study groups achieve greater satisfaction when members develop shared problem perceptions, apply strategies that directly address identified problems, and use regulation strategies frequently. This longitudinal study of 122 university students across 52 groups examined how problem perception homogeneity, strategy immediacy, and strategy intensity predict satisfaction with collaborative learning experiences during exam preparation, confirming all three hypotheses through hierarchical linear modeling.
evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (hierarchical linear modeling of 122 students nested in 52 groups)
coding_notes: Study explicitly uses hierarchical linear modeling to analyze nested data (individuals within groups), making multilevel modeling the primary methodology. Focus on self-regulated strategy use and shared problem perception aligns with self/peer regulation pedagogy. No technology platform mentioned; collaboration is self-organized study groups.

title: Bringing maker practices to school: tracing discursive and materially mediated aspects of student teams’ collaborative making processes
authors: Pirita Seitamaa-Hakkarainen & Kai Hakkarainen & Sini Riikonen
summary_haiku: This study examined how seventh-grade student teams engaged in collaborative making projects using digital and traditional fabrication technologies. Researchers developed the Making-Process-Rug video analysis method to trace social-discursive and materially mediated aspects of five teams' co-invention processes. Four successful teams demonstrated iterative cycles integrating model making with focused discussion, while the unsuccessful team lacked substantive prototyping. Shared epistemic objects and well-organized collaboration processes proved essential for successful co-invention.
evidence_span: methods (Making-Process-Rug video analysis, five teams) + findings (iterative cycles, epistemic objects, collaboration processes)
coding_notes: The study uses micro-analytic video coding of collaborative making episodes (interaction_analysis) combined with discourse analysis of team talk. The focus on how material artifacts (prototypes, digital/traditional fabrication tools) and discursive practices co-constitute learning aligns with distributed cognition and activity theory. Maker projects are open-ended inquiry-based learning with implicit collaboration structures.

title: Finding a place for equity in CSCL: ambitious learning practices as a lever for sustained educational change
authors: Suraj Uttamchandani & Ayesha Bhimdiwala & Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver
summary_haiku: This conceptual article argues that computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) should prioritize educational equity by implementing ambitious learning practices—pedagogies emphasizing collaboration, dialogue, and disciplinary engagement. The authors contend that centering equity through student agency, shared meaning-making, and disruption of social inequality positions CSCL to meaningfully contribute to sustained educational change. They examine adaptive collaborative learning support as a case study, highlighting tensions between technological structure and learner agency while proposing that CSCL innovations can support equitable educational transformation when equity considerations guide development throughout.
evidence_span: abstract, conceptual framing, case study discussion
coding_notes: This is a conceptual/position paper rather than an empirical study, so methodology is inferred from the case study of adaptive collaborative learning support and the emphasis on examining tensions between technology and learner agency. The focus on equity, agency, and disruption of inequality aligns with critical pragmatic theory alongside sociocultural foundations.

title: Encouraging collaboration and building Community in Online Asynchronous Professional Development: designing for social capital
authors: Susan A. Yoon & Katherine Miller & Thomas Richman & Daniel Wendel & Ilana Schoenfeld & Emma Anderson & Jooeun Shim
summary_haiku: This study examined how online asynchronous professional development designed around social capital mechanisms supports science teachers' learning. Eight high school biology teachers participated in a six-week course combining discussion prompts, expert videos, and peer facilitation. Satisfaction surveys showed high ratings across all dimensions. Transactivity analysis revealed that collaborative prompts significantly increased peer interaction compared to content or implementation prompts. Interview data indicated positive perceptions of expertise access and interaction depth, though trust-building remained challenging in the asynchronous format.
evidence_span: methods (transactivity analysis, surveys, interviews) + findings (prompt effects, satisfaction, trust challenges)
coding_notes: Transactivity analysis is a form of interaction coding applied to asynchronous discussion posts; the study systematically codes peer interactions by prompt type, supporting content_analysis as primary. Social capital and community-of-practice framing is explicit. Asynchronous forum is the primary technology; peer facilitation and discussion prompts function as collaboration scripts.

title: Data wrangling practices and collaborative interactions with aggregated data
authors: Shiyan Jiang & Jennifer Kahn
summary_haiku: Youth engaged in data wrangling—selecting and managing large datasets to create models and stories—using interactive visualization tools to explore family migration. Analysis of talk-in-interaction identified ten sociotechnical practices and four learning activity categories: addressing missing data, understanding aggregation, exploring historical events, and varying visual encoding. Collaborative interactions with instructors and peers supported critical inquiry and meaning-making about data's social significance.
evidence_span: methods (talk-in-interaction analysis, coding of practices and activities) + findings (ten sociotechnical practices, four learning categories, collaborative interactions)
coding_notes: Study uses micro-analytic coding of moment-by-moment collaborative episodes around data visualization tools, grounded in sociocultural theory. Secondary methods include discourse analysis of talk and content analysis of identified practices; secondary units include the artifacts (visualizations, datasets) being jointly manipulated.

title: Dialogic intervisualizing in multimodal inquiry
authors: Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver & Lap Ki Chan & Judith L. Green & Susan M. Bridges & Asmalina Saleh
summary_haiku: Medical students collaboratively constructed understanding of cardiovascular physiology through facilitated problem-based learning using multimodal digital texts. Using Interactional Ethnography to analyze one PBL cycle, researchers traced how students iteratively accessed, curated, and generated visual representations—from simple diagrams to complex cardiac cycle charts—within dialogic exchanges with their facilitator. The study proposes "dialogic intervisualizing" as a theoretical construct characterizing dynamic interplay between information problem-solving, textual negotiation, and purposeful dialogue for deep knowledge co-construction in computer-supported inquiry.
evidence_span: methods (Interactional Ethnography, PBL cycle analysis) + findings (dialogic intervisualizing construct, iterative visual representation use)
coding_notes: Study employs fine-grained interaction analysis of collaborative medical students' moment-by-moment dialogue and multimodal artifact use within problem-based learning. Interactional Ethnography is a qualitative, discourse-centered methodology aligned with interaction analysis and ethnographic case study. Primary technology is the shared digital workspace where visual representations are co-constructed; multimodal analysis of texts and dialogue is central.

title: Students’ multimodal knowledge practices in a makerspace learning environment
authors: Anu Kajamaa & Kristiina Kumpulainen
summary_haiku: This sociocultural study examined how students' collaborative knowledge practices are mediated multimodally in a school makerspace during STEAM challenges. Through discourse and multimodal interaction analysis of 350 minutes of video data from two student groups, researchers identified four intertwined knowledge practices: orienting to, interpreting, concretizing, and expanding knowledge. Findings reveal that discourse, materials, embodied actions, and spatial arrangements jointly mediated students' joint attention and knowledge creation, with peer guidance proving more influential than teacher support or pre-given instructions.
evidence_span: methods (video analysis, discourse and multimodal interaction coding) + findings (four knowledge practices, role of materials and embodied actions)
coding_notes: Study employs fine-grained video analysis of moment-by-moment collaborative episodes in a makerspace, coding discourse and multimodal interaction (gestures, materials, spatial positioning). Sociocultural framing emphasizes mediation through multiple semiotic resources; distributed cognition captures how knowledge emerges across people, artifacts, and environment.

title: Social practices in teacher knowledge creation and innovation adoption: a large-scale study in an online instructional design community for inquiry learning
authors: Luis P. Prieto & Tobias Ley & Ton de Jong & Maria Jesus Rodriguez-Triana & Denis Gillet
summary_haiku: This large-scale study analyzed 40,235 inquiry learning designs created in Graasp, an online platform used by 35,000+ teachers, to examine how social practices relate to classroom implementation of pedagogical innovations. Using the Knowledge Appropriation Model framework, researchers found that knowledge maturation, expert scaffolding, and knowledge appropriation practices were significantly associated with increased adoption rates of learning designs in classrooms, with maturation showing the strongest effect.
evidence_span: methods, findings, abstract
coding_notes: Study uses trace data from 40,235 learning designs on Graasp platform to model adoption patterns; Knowledge Appropriation Model and focus on social practices in a large online teacher community align with knowledge-building and distributed cognition frameworks. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

title: Gaze awareness and metacognitive suggestions by a pedagogical conversational agent: an experimental investigation on interventions to support collaborative learning process and performance
authors: Yugo Hayashi
summary_haiku: A 2×2 experimental study examined how real-time gaze feedback and pedagogical conversational agent suggestions independently and jointly affect collaborative learning. Eighty dyads completed a knowledge integration task while receiving various combinations of these interventions. Results showed gaze feedback more effectively facilitated coordination processes, while agent suggestions better improved learning gains. Combined interventions produced synergistic effects on performance, with successful coordination strongly predicting learning outcomes only when both supports were present.
evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (2×2 experimental design), findings (gaze feedback, agent suggestions, synergistic effects)
coding_notes: Study is a controlled 2×2 factorial experiment with dyads as primary unit. Gaze tracking (eye-tracking sensor) and pedagogical conversational agent (LLM-like orchestration providing metacognitive suggestions) are core technologies. Collaboration scripts implicit in structured task and agent prompts. Sociocultural framing evident in focus on coordination and joint learning processes.

title: Give student ideas a larger stage: support cross-community interaction for knowledge building
authors: Guangji Yuan & Maria Bogouslavsky & Jianwei Zhang
summary_haiku: Two grade 5/6 science classrooms engaged in knowledge building about human body systems using Knowledge Forum over ten weeks. Students created "super notes"—synthesized summaries of inquiry progress—as epistemic boundary objects shared in a cross-classroom meta-space. Qualitative analysis revealed students conceived super notes as refined, accessible "big ideas" reflecting their learning journey. Super notes facilitated cross-community interaction, enabling students to encounter diverse perspectives, deepen inquiry, and develop integrated system-level understandings, demonstrating how scaling CSCL practices across classrooms fosters high-level epistemic engagement.
evidence_span: methods, findings, discussion of super notes and cross-classroom interaction
coding_notes: Study is a qualitative, in-depth examination of two classrooms using Knowledge Forum over ten weeks, analyzing how super notes (artifacts) mediate cross-community knowledge building. Primary focus is knowledge-building theory and epistemic engagement; secondary methods include systematic coding of student conceptions and interaction patterns. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

title: A review of the International Handbook of
authors: Jeremy Roschelle
summary_haiku: This review examines the International Handbook of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 2020, analyzing its contributions to the thirty-year-old CSCL field. Using Kuhn's paradigm shift framework, the author identifies the handbook as both a consensus document summarizing established theories, designs, and methods, and a source of productive disequilibria—unresolved tensions in diversity/equity, scalability, learning analytics integration, and methodological coherence—that present opportunities for transformative scholarship and paradigm shifts.
evidence_span: title, abstract, summary
coding_notes: This is a meta-analytic review of a handbook rather than an empirical study of CSCL. The primary methodology is systematic coding and analysis of handbook chapters as artifacts. Pedagogy is not directly applicable since the review examines the field itself rather than implementing a specific pedagogical approach; sociocultural and activity theory are inferred as dominant theoretical frameworks within the reviewed handbook.

title: Promoting regulation of equal participation in online collaboration by combining a group awareness tool and adaptive prompts. But does it even matter?
authors: Sebastian Strauss & Nikol Rummel
summary_haiku: This field experiment examined whether combining a group awareness tool (GAT) with adaptive prompts supports equal participation in online collaborative learning. Sixty-one students in groups received either no support, a GAT alone, or GAT plus prompts. While students showed higher satisfaction with more equal participation, the collaboration support produced only tentative effects on participation equality. Groups initiating collaboration early and coordinating continuously achieved better participation distribution and satisfaction, suggesting interaction patterns matter more than the technological interventions tested.
evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (field experiment with three conditions), findings (participation equality, satisfaction, interaction patterns)
coding_notes: Field experiment with three conditions (control, GAT alone, GAT+prompts) analyzing group-level outcomes (participation equality, satisfaction) and interaction patterns. Group awareness tool and adaptive prompts are core technologies; analysis includes learning traces (participation logs) alongside satisfaction measures. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

title: The spiral model of collaborative knowledge improvement: an exploratory study of a networked collaborative classroom
authors: Wenli Chen & Jesmine S. H. Tan & Zhongling Pi
summary_haiku: This exploratory case study introduces the Spiral Model of Collaborative Knowledge Improvement (SMCKI), a five-phase pedagogical framework designed to scaffold multi-layered collaborative learning in networked classrooms. Pre-service teachers collaboratively designed technology-enhanced learning activities through individual ideation, intra-group synergy, inter-group critique, intra-group refinement, and individual achievement phases. Results demonstrate significant quality improvements in technology-enhanced learning designs across all SMCKI phases, with participants progressively advancing from simple to complex knowledge dimensions.
evidence_span: title, abstract, methods, findings
coding_notes: The SMCKI framework is a structured, iterative pedagogical intervention studied in a networked classroom context with phases scaffolding individual and collaborative refinement of designs. The five-phase model with critique and refinement cycles aligns with knowledge-building principles and collaboration scripts. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

title: Capturing regulatory patterns in online collaborative learning: A network analytic approach
authors: Si Zhang & Juan Chen & Yun Wen & Hongxian Chen & Qianqian Gao & Qiyun Wang
summary_haiku: This study examined 45 student teachers' regulatory patterns during online collaborative learning using content analysis and epistemic network analysis (ENA). Findings revealed that high-performing groups demonstrated significantly more content monitoring and emotional regulation behaviors than low-performing groups across different activity stages. The analysis identified distinct regulatory patterns: high-performing groups emphasized planning and evaluation, while low-performing groups relied on routine-level regulatory strategies throughout collaboration.
evidence_span: title, methods (content analysis and epistemic network analysis), findings (regulatory patterns across groups and stages)
coding_notes: Epistemic network analysis (ENA) is a graph-based method for visualizing and analyzing connections among concepts in discourse, making social_network_analysis the primary methodology. The study uses content analysis to code regulatory behaviors and ENA to map their relational patterns. Unit of analysis is small groups (45 student teachers in collaborative teams), with cross-level analysis comparing high vs. low-performing groups. Self-regulation and peer regulation are central to the pedagogical focus.

title: Affording embodied cognition through touchscreen and above-the-surface gestures during collaborative tabletop science learning
authors: Nikita Soni
summary_haiku: This study examined how family groups use touchscreen and above-the-surface gestures during collaborative learning with multi-touch tabletops displaying ocean temperature data. Using a user-centered design approach, researchers analyzed 11 family groups' utterances and gestures to identify embodied cognition instances. Four gesture types emerged: orienting the group, cooperative gestures, individual intentional gestures, and articulating conceptual understanding. Findings reveal specific gestural interactions that facilitate embodied-cognition-supported collaborative meaning-making in science learning.
evidence_span: title, abstract, methods, findings
coding_notes: Study uses micro-analytic coding of moment-by-moment gestures and utterances during collaborative tabletop interaction. Multimodal analysis of touchscreen and above-the-surface gestures captures embodied cognition; design-based approach with family groups as primary analytical unit. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

title: Initiating scientific collaborations across career levels and disciplines – a network analysis on behavioral data
authors: Julia Eberle & Karsten Stegmann & Alain Barrat & Frank Fischer & Kristine Lund
summary_haiku: This study examined how researchers initiate scientific collaborations at face-to-face academic events using network analysis of behavioral data. Analyzing 5,736 relations among 287 researchers at two technology-enhanced learning conferences, the researchers employed RFID devices to measure contact duration and social network questionnaires to identify collaboration intentions. Results revealed that longer face-to-face contact, reciprocity, and transitivity significantly predicted new collaboration formation. PhD students were less frequently selected as partners, and Information Technology researchers selected fewer partners overall. Group awareness support reduced disciplinary differences in partner selection, suggesting targeted interventions can facilitate interdisciplinary collaboration.
evidence_span: methods (RFID, network questionnaires, 287 researchers, 5,736 relations) + findings (contact duration, reciprocity, transitivity predicting collaboration; career-level and disciplinary effects; group awareness support)
coding_notes: Primary methodology is social network analysis (graph-based analysis of interaction ties and centrality metrics). RFID sensors and questionnaires capture behavioral and relational data at a large-scale academic community. Group awareness support is the technology intervention, with RFID as a sensor modality. Theory emphasizes distributed cognition across the research community and communities of practice lens on collaboration formation.

title: Improving learning and writing outcomes: Influence of cognitive and behavioral group awareness tools in wikis
authors: Lisa Ollesch & Sven Heimbuch & Daniel Bodemer
summary_haiku: This study examined how cognitive and behavioral group awareness tools affect wiki-based collaborative learning through a 2×2 factorial experiment with 158 participants. Results show both tool types influence thread selection and discussion engagement, with behavioral awareness particularly motivating contributions. Critically, only the combination of cognitive and behavioral awareness improved article quality, suggesting complementary effects outweigh individual benefits in supporting wiki-based learning outcomes.
evidence_span: methods (2×2 factorial design, 158 participants) + findings (tool effects on thread selection, engagement, article quality)
coding_notes: Study uses controlled factorial experiment comparing awareness tool conditions in wiki-based collaboration. Primary unit is small groups collaborating on wiki articles; secondary focus on artifact quality (article outcomes). Awareness tools function as structured scaffolds guiding collaborative behavior and cognition.

title: Guidance in computer‑supported collaborative inquiry learning: Capturing aspects of affect and teacher support in science classrooms
authors: Tarja Pietarinen & Tuire Palonen & Marja Vauras
summary_haiku: Teachers in computer-supported collaborative science inquiry learning primarily focused on task management and content knowledge while extensively observing groups. Mixed-methods analysis of four classrooms revealed teachers preferentially guided groups perceived as motivated and collaborative, regardless of prior competence. Notably, socio-emotional support was minimal. Teachers' positive affect correlated with student affect, suggesting reciprocal emotional influences on learning outcomes.
evidence_span: methods + findings; teacher guidance patterns, affect analysis, group observation
coding_notes: Study combines quantitative observation frequencies and qualitative interaction coding across four classrooms. Primary focus on teacher facilitation decisions and affect dynamics during computer-supported inquiry; secondary units include small-group collaboration and cross-level analysis of teacher–student emotional reciprocity.

title: Net.Create: Network Visualization to Support Collaborative Historical Knowledge Building
authors: Kalani Craig & Joshua Danish & Megan Humburg & Cindy Hmelo-Silver & Maksymilian Szostalo & Ann McCranie
summary_haiku: # Summary This study examines Net.Create, a collaborative network visualization tool designed to help undergraduate history students analyze complex texts. Using activity theory, researchers analyzed how the tool and accompanying activities help students reconcile contradictions between detail and context, active learning and large lectures, and memorization versus historical reasoning. Analysis of log data, video recordings, and student papers from 76 students reveals that quality of historical significance annotations—not quantity of entries—correlates with stronger final papers. Students successfully moved between local details and aggregate patterns, with high-performing groups engaging in deeper "why" analysis compared to low-performing groups focused on "who" and "what."
evidence_span: methods (log data, video, student papers) + findings (annotation quality, group performance patterns)
coding_notes: Primary methodology is learning_analytics because trace data (logs) from the digital platform are used to model learning outcomes (paper quality, group performance). Activity theory is the explicit theoretical frame; knowledge_building_theory is secondary because the tool supports collaborative knowledge construction about historical significance. Net.Create is a network visualization and co-editing workspace, classified as shared_workspace_canvas with awareness features.

title: Social sensitivity: a manifesto for CSCL research
authors: Jaana Isohatala & Piia Naykki & Sanna Jarvela & Michael J. Baker & Kristine Lund
summary_haiku: Current educational technologies inadequately support collaborative learning as both cognitive and socio-emotional processes, risking hindered idea exchange and negative interactions. This manifesto argues CSCL research is fragmented across theoretical silos, failing to communicate coherent evidence to practitioners and developers. The authors propose "social sensitivity"—an interdisciplinary framework emphasizing constructively critical, respectful, and cohesive collaboration—and call for concrete actions: crossing theoretical boundaries, conducting multimodal empirical research, and transferring evidence to educational practices and policies.
evidence_span: abstract and framing; manifesto/position paper
coding_notes: This is a manifesto and position paper rather than an empirical study, so methodology and unit of analysis do not fit standard research designs. The work advocates for social sensitivity in CSCL—emphasizing respectful, cohesive, and constructively critical collaboration—which aligns with collaboration scripts and self-regulation. Theory draws on sociocultural, dialogic, and socio-cognitive traditions to frame the need for integrating cognitive and socio-emotional processes.

title: Deconstructing orchestration load: comparing teacher support through mirroring and guiding
authors: Ishari Amarasinghe & Davinia Hernandez-Leo & H. Ulrich Hoppe
summary_haiku: This study compared how mirroring and guiding support in teacher dashboards influence orchestration load during scripted collaborative learning. Six teachers conducted Pyramid-pattern activities under three conditions: no dashboard, mirroring support, and guiding support with alerts. Using epistemic network analysis, researchers found that guiding support enabled more targeted interactions and announcements compared to mirroring support. The findings deconstruct orchestration load into situation evaluation, goal formation, and action-taking facets.
evidence_span: methods (epistemic network analysis, dashboard conditions) + findings (orchestration load facets, interaction patterns)
coding_notes: The study uses epistemic network analysis to examine teacher orchestration moves across dashboard conditions, focusing on how awareness tools mediate teacher decision-making during scripted collaborative activities. Primary focus is teacher facilitation and orchestration load rather than learner outcomes.

title: Prompting collaborative and exploratory discourse: An epistemic network analysis study
authors: Zarifa Zakaria & Jennifer Tsan & Anna Iwanski & Jessica Vandenberg & Collin Lynch & Kristy Elizabeth Boyer & Eric Wiebe
summary_haiku: This study examined how simple prompting interventions affect elementary students' collaborative discourse during pair programming. Using Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) to analyze coded dialogue from 62 fourth graders, researchers compared intervention students receiving empirically-derived prompts supporting exploratory talk with control students. Results revealed intervention students significantly increased justification, alternative ideas, and simple questions, demonstrating qualitatively different collaboration patterns through network visualizations showing stronger connections between exploratory talk codes.
evidence_span: methods (ENA coding of dialogue, intervention design) + findings (network visualizations, discourse pattern comparisons)
coding_notes: Primary methodology is interaction_analysis because the study codes and analyzes moment-by-moment collaborative dialogue; ENA is a secondary social_network_analysis method applied to those coded interactions. Prompting intervention is a collaboration_script that structures exploratory talk. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

title: The impact of a gamified mobile question‑asking app on museum visitor group interactions: an ICAP framing
authors: Jesse Ha & Luis E. Perez Cortes & Man Su & Brian C. Nelson & Catherine Bowman & Judd D. Bowman
summary_haiku: This study examined how a gamified mobile question-asking app affects museum visitor group interactions using the ICAP framework. Researchers compared two app modes—Ask Mode (baseline) and Game Mode (gamified)—across 1,539 visitor groups at two museums. Results showed gamified versions significantly increased group discussion frequency and collaborative question-asking, particularly among family groups and when children controlled the device, supporting mobile apps' potential for fostering informal collaborative learning.
evidence_span: methods (comparison of Ask Mode vs. Game Mode), findings (group discussion frequency, collaborative question-asking)
coding_notes: Study compares two app conditions (quasi-experimental design) with large sample of visitor groups (n=1,539). ICAP framework guides analysis of collaborative interaction quality. Technology is a mobile app supporting question-asking; classified as synchronous because real-time group interaction is the focus, though awareness/gamification elements also present. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

title: Agency to transform: how did a grade 5 community co‑configure dynamic knowledge building practices in a yearlong science inquiry?
authors: Dan Tao & Jianwei Zhang
summary_haiku: This study investigates how a fifth-grade science classroom co-configured dynamic knowledge-building practices through "reflective structuration"—a process where students and teacher collaboratively constructed and adapted shared inquiry structures over a yearlong human body systems investigation. Using qualitative analysis of classroom observations, online discourse, and student artifacts, researchers documented how students co-formulated nine evolving "big questions" that guided inquiry directions. Analysis revealed students' agentic moves expanded, deepened, and reframed collective work, with social network analysis and pre-post testing demonstrating productive knowledge building outcomes and improved scientific understanding.
evidence_span: methods, findings, yearlong intervention design
coding_notes: Study exemplifies design-based research with iterative co-configuration of inquiry structures over a full school year. Primary methodology is design-based; interaction analysis and social network analysis are secondary analytic methods. Knowledge building theory and sociocultural framing are explicit; activity theory applies to the structuration process. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

title: Modelling diffusion in computer-supported collaborative learning: a large scale learning analytics study
authors: Mohammed Saqr & Sonsoles Lopez-Pernas
summary_haiku: This large-scale study of 69 courses (3,277 students) examines whether diffusion-based network centrality measures capture information exchange and predict academic success in computer-supported collaborative learning. Using meta-analysis across all courses, the research demonstrates that diffusion centralities—measuring how ideas spread through networks—show stronger and more consistent correlations with student achievement than traditional network measures. Clustering analysis identified three student roles: influencers, mediators, and isolates, validated through manual coding of interactions.
evidence_span: title, abstract, methods, findings
coding_notes: Study employs social network analysis with diffusion-based centrality measures on large-scale CSCL trace data (69 courses, 3,277 students) to model information exchange and predict achievement. Learning analytics and descriptive statistics support the primary SNA methodology. Unit of analysis is the network community with secondary focus on individual learner outcomes. Distributed cognition theory aligns with diffusion and information-spread framing; sociocultural perspective implicit in collaborative learning context.

title: Many are the ways to learn identifying multi-modal behavioral profiles of collaborative learning in constructivist activities
authors: Jauwairia Nasir & Aditi Kothiyal & Barbara Bruno
summary_haiku: This study identifies three distinct multi-modal behavioral profiles of dyads engaged in collaborative open-ended learning with interactive tabletops and a robot mediator. Using combined learning analytics and interaction analysis on video, audio, and log data from 32 teams, researchers discovered two learning profiles—Expressive Explorers and Calm Tinkerers—and one non-learning profile, Silent Wanderers. Key findings reveal that speech overlap and reflection behaviors strongly distinguish learners from non-learners, while problem-solving strategy interacts with emotional expressivity to characterize different pathways to learning.
evidence_span: methods (video, audio, log data; interaction analysis; learning analytics) + findings (behavioral profiles; speech overlap; reflection behaviors)
coding_notes: Study combines micro-analytic coding of collaborative episodes (interaction_analysis) with trace data from tabletop and robot (learning_analytics, multimodal sensors). Primary unit is dyads; open-ended constructivist activity aligns with inquiry-based pedagogy. Sociocultural framing evident in focus on collaborative meaning-making and distributed cognition across human-robot-artifact system.

title: Self‑efficacy and behavior patterns of learners using a real‑time collaboration system developed for group programming
authors: Ting-Chia Hsu & Hal Abelson & Evan Patton & Shih-Chu Chen & Hsuan-Ning Chang
summary_haiku: This study examined how adult learners' self-efficacy and collaborative behaviors differ when using a real-time collaboration (RTC) system integrated with MIT App Inventor for block-based programming. Using sequential behavior analysis on 13 participants grouped by disciplinary background, researchers found that RTC enabled simultaneous task execution and enhanced communication through annotations. Computer Science majors in homogeneous groups demonstrated significantly higher programming self-efficacy during collaboration than non-majors and heterogeneous groups, though individual versus collaborative self-efficacy remained comparable overall.
evidence_span: methods (sequential behavior analysis, participant grouping) + findings (self-efficacy differences, behavior patterns)
coding_notes: Primary methodology is sequence_process_mining because the study explicitly uses sequential behavior analysis to extract temporal patterns from collaborative episodes. The RTC system with annotations and simultaneous task execution is a shared workspace; self-efficacy measurement and group composition analysis support secondary descriptive and interaction-analytic methods.

title: The trade‑off between individuals and groups: role interactions under different technology affordance conditions
authors: Cixiao Wang & Shuling Li
summary_haiku: This study examined how technology affordances—specifically device-to-student ratios (1:1 versus 1:m) and external scripts—influence role-based interactions during collaborative scientific inquiry. Using thematic analysis, descriptive statistics, and social network analysis with 130 fifth-grade students across three inquiry experiments, researchers identified eleven emergent roles organized into five categories. Key findings revealed that limited technology resources and external scripts promoted collective awareness, while personal device ownership encouraged individual-focused behavior. Stable group action orientations facilitated better coordination and learning outcomes, though close interaction density did not guarantee collaborative effectiveness.
evidence_span: methods (thematic analysis, SNA, descriptive statistics) + findings (role interactions, group coordination, learning outcomes)
coding_notes: Primary methodology is social network analysis of role-based interactions; secondary methods include thematic coding (content analysis) and descriptive statistics. Study examines both individual roles and group-level coordination under different technology affordances, supporting cross-level analysis. External scripts and device ratios are core pedagogical manipulations.

title: Educational dialogues and computer supported collaborative learning: critical analysis and research perspectives
authors: Michael J. Baker & Baruch B. Schwarz & Sten R. Ludvigsen
summary_haiku: This critical analysis proposes that educational dialogue research in CSCL requires theoretically grounded integration of diverse data types across multiple timescales. The authors argue the object of study should be collective thinking development in dialogue, with the exchange as the basic analytical unit. They introduce digital platforms as an intermediary analytical level between micro-dialogic exchanges and macro-institutional contexts, emphasizing the need for coherent theoretical frameworks connecting automatic and human analyses to avoid fragmentation.
evidence_span: abstract, introduction, and theoretical framing sections
coding_notes: This is a critical analysis and research perspective paper rather than an empirical study. The focus on educational dialogue, exchange as analytical unit, and integration of micro-dialogic and macro-institutional levels strongly indicates discourse and interaction analysis grounded in dialogic theory. The emphasis on digital platforms as intermediary analytical level suggests multi-level analysis across timescales.

title: Integrating collaboration scripts, group awareness, and self‑regulation in computer‑supported collaborative learning
authors: Lenka Schnaubert & Freydis Vogel
summary_haiku: This special issue examines three interconnected concepts in computer-supported collaborative learning: group awareness, collaboration scripts, and self-regulation. Through conceptual and empirical papers, the collection explores how these mechanisms—which support learners' social interactions, cognitive processes, and metacognitive monitoring—can be combined to enhance collaborative learning design. The papers demonstrate that integrating these approaches yields more effective CSCL environments than addressing them separately.
evidence_span: title, abstract, special issue framing
coding_notes: This is a special issue editorial/overview synthesizing multiple empirical and conceptual papers on collaboration scripts, group awareness, and self-regulation in CSCL. Primary methodology coded as mixed_methods because the collection integrates both conceptual and empirical work; confidence is moderate because the summary does not detail specific methodologies of individual papers. Pedagogy and technology reflect the three core mechanisms highlighted (scripts, awareness, self-regulation).

title: Group awareness and regulation in
authors: Lenka Schnaubert & Daniel Bodemer
summary_haiku: This article conceptualizes group awareness (GA) in computer-supported collaborative learning as a conscious, current, individual cognitive construct about social entities that learners perceive as valid. The authors identify six defining aspects of GA and propose it operates within three regulatory cycles: regulating GA itself through metacognitive monitoring, regulating social interaction based on GA, and regulating partner schema building. The framework connects GA to working memory processes and suggests implications for designing support tools and conducting empirical research on collaborative learning mechanisms.
evidence_span: abstract and conceptual framework; no empirical data reported
coding_notes: This is a conceptual/theoretical paper proposing a framework for group awareness and regulatory cycles in CSCL. It does not report empirical data collection or analysis; instead, it synthesizes existing literature and proposes a model. Coded as content_analysis (systematic conceptual decomposition) with discourse_analysis as secondary because the framework addresses how awareness and regulation operate through interaction. Technology is coded as awareness_dashboard because the paper discusses implications for designing support tools that make group activity visible.

title: Adaptable scaffolding of mathematical argumentation skills: The role of self‑regulation when scaffolded with CSCL scripts and heuristic worked examples
authors: Freydis Vogel & Ingo Kollar & Frank Fischer & Kristina Reiss & Stefan Ufer
summary_haiku: Two experiments examined adaptable versus non-adaptable scaffolding for mathematical argumentation skills in collaborative learning. University students (N=167) learned with either adaptable or fixed CSCL scripts and heuristic worked examples. Results showed maximal scaffolding supported domain-specific skills, while adaptable scaffolds benefited students with higher self-regulation abilities. Self-regulation skills proved crucial for effectively utilizing adaptable scaffolding, particularly for socio-discursive argumentation development.
evidence_span: title, abstract, methods, results
coding_notes: Two-condition experimental design comparing adaptable vs. fixed CSCL scripts with worked examples. Primary focus on collaboration scripts and self-regulation as moderator of scaffolding effectiveness. Sociocultural framing evident in emphasis on socio-discursive argumentation development within collaborative dyads.

title: ‘Supporting socially shared regulation during collaborative task‑oriented reading’
authors: Jolique Kielstra & Inge Molenaar & Roel van Steensel & Ludo Verhoeven
summary_haiku: A collaboration script designed to support socially shared regulation during task-oriented reading facilitated mainly low-level metacognitive discussions among 44 prevocational students working in groups. While the script elicited metacognitive regulation through role-based information distribution, deep-level co-construction remained rare. However, students individually improved their ability to recognize high-level task characteristics and reflect on appropriate reading strategies post-intervention.
evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (44 students, groups, script intervention), findings (metacognitive discussions, individual post-intervention gains)
coding_notes: Study employs a collaboration script intervention with 44 prevocational students in small groups, examining socially shared regulation during reading. Interaction analysis of metacognitive discussions and content analysis of task-oriented talk are evident. Primary focus is on group-level regulation processes, with secondary attention to individual learning outcomes post-intervention.

title: CSsCL: the performance of collaborative learning
authors: Charles Crook
summary_haiku: This commentary examines three foundational concepts in computer-supported collaborative learning: collaboration scripts, self-regulation, and group awareness. Through analysis of five special issue papers, Crook proposes that regulation operates in layered structures requiring "meta-metacognition," and that group awareness involves both social cognition and intersubjectivity. He reconceptualizes scripted collaboration using a theatre metaphor, emphasizing performance, direction, and audience perspectives to better integrate these concepts within classroom ecosystems.
evidence_span: abstract, commentary structure, conceptual analysis of five papers
coding_notes: This is a commentary/review article that systematically examines and reconceptualizes three foundational CSCL concepts through analysis of published papers. The primary methodology is content analysis of existing literature combined with discourse-level conceptual work. The unit of analysis is the published papers and their ideas (artifacts), though the commentary addresses classroom-level implications. Technology is not the focus; the work is theoretical and conceptual.

title: Integrating a collaboration script and group awareness to support group regulation and emotions towards collaborative problem solving
authors: Matias Rojas & Miguel Nussbaum & Orlando Guerrero & Pablo Chiuminatto & Samuel Greiff & Rodrigo Del Rio & Danilo Alvares
summary_haiku: This study examined how a game-based collaboration script with group awareness tools affects elementary students' collaborative problem-solving skills. Using a quasi-experimental design with 223 sixth-graders, researchers compared an experimental group playing a six-level collaborative game to a control group receiving regular instruction. Results showed the intervention significantly improved attitudes toward collaboration and increased shared regulation and co-regulation processes. Qualitative analysis revealed positive emotions like satisfaction emerged through co-regulation, suggesting collaboration scripts combined with group awareness effectively support regulation skills and emotional development during collaborative problem-solving.
evidence_span: methods (quasi-experimental design, 223 sixth-graders, experimental vs. control), findings (attitudes, shared regulation, co-regulation, emotions)
coding_notes: Study uses a game-based collaboration script with group awareness tools in a quasi-experimental design. Primary focus is on how structured collaboration scripts and awareness mechanisms support group regulation and emotions. Qualitative analysis of emotions and regulation processes complements quantitative outcome measures.

title: Supporting children’s place-based observations and explanations using collaboration scripts while learning-on- the-move outdoors
authors: Heather Toomey Zimmerman & Susan M. Land
summary_haiku: This design-based research study examined how collaboration scripts embedded in a mobile augmented reality app supported children's learning during outdoor activities. Across two iterations with 87 youth participants, researchers found significant gains in tree life cycle knowledge for both groups. Iteration B, which included additional scripts for socially-shared regulation of learning, showed improved collaborative sense-making where children better coordinated observational evidence with explanations, though knowledge gains were comparable between iterations.
evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (design-based iterations), findings (knowledge gains, collaborative sense-making)
coding_notes: Design-based research with two iterative cycles testing collaboration scripts in a mobile AR app. Primary focus on dyadic/small-group collaboration during outdoor learning; secondary attention to individual knowledge outcomes. Sociocultural framing evident in emphasis on socially-shared regulation and collaborative sense-making.

title: Patterns of action transitions in online collaborative problem solving: A network analysis approach
authors: Shupin Li & Johanna Poysa-Tarhonen & Paivi Hakkinen
summary_haiku: This study examined 166 Finnish sixth graders' action transition patterns during computer-based collaborative problem-solving using social network analysis. Researchers created transition networks from log file data and calculated network measures including density, centralization, and reciprocity. Results showed pairs with at least one member possessing high social and cognitive skills conducted significantly more actions with higher transition frequencies, suggesting more productive collaborative problem-solving than other pair compositions.
evidence_span: methods + findings
coding_notes: Study uses graph-based network analysis (density, centralization, reciprocity) on action transition patterns from log data, with learning analytics as secondary method. Primary unit is dyad pairs, though individual skill composition is also analyzed. Computer-based problem-solving environment suggests shared workspace technology.

title: Collaborative analytics-supported reflective Assessment for Scaffolding Pre-service Teachers’ collaborative Inquiry and Knowledge Building
authors: Yuqin Yang & Gaoxia Zhu & Daner Sun & Carol K. K. Chan
summary_haiku: This study examined how collaborative analytics-supported reflective assessment enhances pre-service teachers' competencies in collaborative inquiry and knowledge building. Using a quasi-experimental design with 40 experimental and 28 comparison pre-service teachers over 18 weeks, the experimental group engaged in knowledge building enriched by KBDeX visualizations and rubrics, while the comparison group used portfolio assessment. Analysis of Knowledge Forum discourse revealed that the experimental group demonstrated significantly higher-level epistemic engagement, collaborative interactions, and metacognitive reflection. Epistemic network analysis showed stronger connections between higher-level actions in the experimental group, and cumulative degree centrality indicated greater community knowledge advancement. Results suggest collaborative analytics-supported reflective assessment effectively scaffolds pre-service teachers' development of collaborative inquiry competencies.
evidence_span: methods (quasi-experimental design, 18-week intervention, Knowledge Forum discourse analysis, epistemic network analysis) + findings (higher epistemic engagement, stronger network connections, centrality measures)
coding_notes: Study combines quantitative comparison (quasi-experimental with control group) and qualitative discourse/network analysis of Knowledge Forum interactions. Primary focus is knowledge building pedagogy scaffolded by collaborative analytics (KBDeX visualizations and rubrics). Epistemic network analysis and cumulative degree centrality are secondary quantitative methods applied to discourse data.

title: A classification of Challenges encountered in Complex Teamwork Settings
authors: Maedeh A. Kazemitabar & Susanne P. Lajoie & Tianshu Li
summary_haiku: This study examined teamwork challenges in a computer-supported collaborative learning environment using a hackathon as the research context. Through multimodal data collection including questionnaires, interviews, and video recordings of 48 participants, researchers employed qualitative theory-driven coding to identify 16 distinct challenges. These challenges were categorized into seven macro-level themes: cognitive, motivational, emotional, behavioral, cognitive/behavioral, general, and external.
