Technology spans shared workspaces (lab simulations), synchronous tools, and awareness features. No AI/LLM involvement in the review or technologies reviewed.

title: Learning to deal with hate speech: An online collective intelligence experiment on the Collective Learning platform
authors: Tatiana Iniguez-Berrozpe & Carmen Elboj-Saso & Francesco Marcaletti
summary_haiku: This study examined whether collective intelligence can help adolescents manage online hate speech using the Collective Learning platform. Spanish teenagers (ages 15–16) were divided into one large group (n=123) and two smaller groups (n=18, n=23). Results showed that collective intelligence conditions emerged only in the large group, which demonstrated significant improvements in responses across four questions assessing moral reasoning and prosocial action regarding hate speech. Small groups showed minimal improvement, suggesting group size and heterogeneity are critical for collective intelligence to facilitate learning about hate speech prevention.

However, challenges including negative tone, bias, and occasional incoherence could undermine dialogue and require computational and pedagogical solutions.

authors: Sarah Jaewon Lee & Xintian Tu & Simeon Adebola & D. Teo Keifert & Noel Enyedy & Joshua Danish

Using interaction analysis of three episodes (making solid, liquid, and gas bonds), researchers found that children progressively blended diverse feedback modalities to collectively construct scientific understanding while exercising agency over their inquiry process. The findings demonstrate that embodied, technology-enhanced environments supporting collective feedback structures enable young children to engage in sophisticated systems thinking earlier than traditionally expected.

Analyzing 18 student triads, findings reveal prior knowledge supports individual task execution but requires strong leadership for collaborative engagement. Interactive discourse modes foster significantly richer engagement and higher achievement than active modes, with social engagement and emotional regulation emerging as primary predictors of learning outcomes.

title: A quarter century of advances in collaboration sensing: a comprehensive review of high‑frequency metrics and their connection to collaborative constructs from 2000 to 2025

Key findings reveal most studies employed laboratory settings with small samples, relied on simple synchronization metrics, and lacked standardized measurement tools. Critically, less than 9% leveraged sensor data for real-time interventions, identifying major gaps in designing guidance systems beyond mirroring feedback.

title: Understanding when anger becomes productive or destructive in collaborative educational games
authors: Taehyun Kim & Mike Tissenbaum

However, when anger escalates into "tilting"—characterized by emotional dysregulation, withdrawal, and abandonment of collaborative goals—it severely disrupts group performance. The study analyzed middle school students' interactions in City Settlers, finding that appropriately expressed anger drove deeper engagement with complex systems, while unresolved anger conflicts led to group breakdown.

Findings reveal that synthesis artifacts guided discourse progression, enabled key knowledge practices, and supported group artifact development, though effectiveness depended on both artifact quality and collaborative engagement patterns.

title: A temporal network approach to reveal the longitudinal dynamics of CSCL group regulation and productive collaboration

Analyzing 118 discussion groups, researchers identified four distinct weekly regulation patterns and found that groups using interactive socioemotional or regulated constructive patterns demonstrated higher cognitive productivity. Critically, explicit group regulation emerged infrequently and primarily in response to challenges, while most groups maintained stable patterns with minimal improvement over time, suggesting early instructional support is essential for fostering productive regulation.

Through workshops with 17 families, researchers found that collaborative learning emerges via material interaction and shared problem-solving, with family roles dynamically shifting. Rather than traditional adult-to-child knowledge transfer, findings reveal multidirectional zones of proximal development where children, parents, and digital artifacts alternately serve as "more knowledgeable others," enabling intergenerational co-construction of understanding about datafication and algorithmic systems.
